TITLE: New York Climate Exchange Climate Tech Fellowship 2026 ($10,000 stipend)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 1, 2026

Applications are invited for the New York Climate Exchange Climate Tech Fellowship 2026. The Climate Tech Fellowship is a six-month hybrid program that combines expert-led curriculum, 1:1 mentorship, non-dilutive funding, and access to The Exchange’s global partner ecosystem.

Fellows leave with a clearer commercialization roadmap, stronger fundraising readiness, and a network of mentors, peers, and potential investors. Building on a successful inaugural cohort in 2025, the 2026 Fellowship, supported by NYSERDA, is dedicated to a specific and urgent theme at the intersection of Energy & Urban Resilience.

Benefits

Each fellow gains access to a curated set of resources designed to accelerate their path from promising concept to viable venture:

$10,000 non-dilutive stipend (per team)

Structured go-to-market curriculum covering market mapping, customer segmentation, target markets, channels, and commercialization strategy — taught by expert instructors

Expert sessions on fundraising, IP strategy, communications, and climate equity

Dedicated 1:1 mentorship sessions, matched to specific focus area and stage of development

A personalized Fellowship blueprint and tailored roadmap with monthly check-ins to track progress

In-person programming during Climate Week NYC in September, including a showcase for investors and partners. Travel and accommodation for one team member will be covered

Introductions to investors, policymakers, and strategic partners through The Exchange’s global network

Eligibility

The Fellowship is designed for early-stage innovators — researchers, scientists, engineers, and entrepreneurs — who are working on energy technologies with meaningful urban resilience potential. You are a strong fit if:

Your work addresses Energy & Urban Resilience

You are at the prototype, early pilot, or early commercialization stage

You are looking for more than grant funding (i.e., you want structured support with commercialization strategy, customer discovery, and venture building)

You can commit several hours per week to the program over six months from September 2026-February 2027

University or institutional affiliation is not required. The Fellowship is open to innovators globally. Incorporation is not required. The program is specifically designed for innovators at the pre-company formation to pre-seed stage. They particularly encourage applications from founders from underrepresented backgrounds.

Application

Innovators interested should complete the online form, and provide details on the innovation, goals for the Fellowship, and team. They will review applications on a rolling basis, so apply early.

Click here to apply

For more information, visit Climate Tech Fellowship.

TITLE: D-Prize Global Competition 2026 for Entrepreneurs ($20K grants)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: December 6, 2026

Applications are open for the D-Prize Global Competition 2026. The D-Prize awards startup grants of up to $20,000 to entrepreneurs launching new organizations. They believe the world needs more social impact organizations, and they seed for-profit ventures, NGOs, and charities. They support organizations in any low-or-middle income country where extreme poverty still exists.

They believe social impact organizations are uniquely positioned to distribute an existing product or service known to improve lives where need still exists.

Challenges

Childhood Diarrhea Treatment: Can you get free ORS and zinc into homes before a child gets sick and prevent one of the leading killers of children under five?

DMPA-SC: Reach Underserved Populations: Can you distribute DMPA-SC to underserved population?

DMPA-SC: Improve Provider Training: Can you improve mandatory provider training for DMPA-SC?

DMPA-SC: Last Mile Inventory Management: Can you improve last mile inventory management of DMPA-SC?

DMPA-SC: Medical Waste Management: Can you increase safe disposal of DMPA-SC needles?

Reading Glasses: Can you distribute non-prescription reading/ working glasses to those in need?

Childcare: Can you help low-income families access quality childcare services?

ConnectEd Phone-based Tutoring: Can you distribute a phone-based intervention to improve learning?

Teaching at the Right Level: Can you improve foundational literacy and numeracy in resource-limited classrooms?

Road Safety: Can you reduce road deaths by replicating a proven public transport safety campaign?

Government Transparency: Can you monitor and report data to reduce corruption and improve public service?

Poverty Graduation: Can you provide coaching, capital, and social support to lift people out of ultra poverty?

Agriculture: Propose Your Own: Propose distribution of an evidence-based agriculture intervention not on the list.

Post-Harvest Support: Can you provide post-harvest loans and storage technology proven to smallholders?

Quality Inputs: Can you provide smallholders quality inputs and training to increase their harvests?

Water Filters: Can you sell ceramic water filters to people in areas without access to clean water?

Kangaroo Care: Can you provide access to Kangaroo Care (KC), a proven but underused intervention for infants born too soon or too small?

Oxygen: Can you develop a team of technicians to service and repair existing oxygen concentrators to improve access to medical oxygen?

Patient Identification: Can you develop a way to identify patients needing treatment for either obstetric fistula, cervical cancer, club foot, or cataracts, then connect them with existing treatment services in your area?

Maternal Health: Can you train birth attendants to administer misoprostol to prevent maternal deaths from postpartum hemorrhaging?

Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission: Can you counsel and motivate HIV-positive pregnant women to adhere to their ART regimen, and thus prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission?

Child Immunization: Can you direct caregivers to bring children to health facilities for routine immunizations that would otherwise not occur?

Sugar Daddy Awareness: Can you teach Sugar Daddy Awareness to 8th grade classes to reduce unwanted teen pregnancies and HIV infections?

Propose your own: Pitch distribution of an intervention backed by credible evidence and not on the list.

Eligibility

New organizations only. Most awardees are first-time entrepreneurs who have not yet launched or raised outside funding.

They especially encourage applicants from low- and middle-income countries.

Orgs with more than 18 months of full-time operations or more than $30,000 USD raised typically not supported.

Existing organizations considered only if your core focus is distributing an existing, evidence-based poverty intervention.

Application

Select an intervention and be prepared for the following deadlines:

The Global Competition launches on 14 September 2026

Early Submission Deadline: 25 October 2026 at midnight PT (Pacific Time)

Regular Submission Deadline: 15 November 2026 at midnight PT (Pacific Time)

Extension Deadline: 6 December 2026 at midnight PT (Pacific Time)

For more information, visit D-Prize Global Competition.

MIASA Individual Fellowships (Junior/Senior) at University of Ghana 2023/2024 for African Scholars

MIASA Fellowships are now open. Call for Applications for Individual Residential Fellowships for 3-12 months each at the University of Ghana

Application Deadline: 30th September 2022, 11:59pm UTC

Eligible Countries: African countries

About the Award:

The Maria Sibylla Merian Institute for Advanced Studies in Africa (MIASA) is dedicated to research in the Humanities and Social Sciences, with ‘Sustainable Governance’ as its central topic. Our main thematic corridors are conflict and sustainable peace, democracy and environmental transformation. We are also interested in a wide range of intersectional sub-topics, such as landownership and acquisition, migration and mobility, restitution of cultural objects, African cities, human rights and other related themes.

The present call is for up to ten (10) individual residential fellowships for 3-12 months each for the academic year 2023/2024. The starting date of a fellowship is generally handled flexibly, however, we strongly encourage to set the starting date on either 1st of June 2023, 1st of August 2023 or 1st of January 2024. The latest possible date for the end of a fellowship is the 31st of July 2024.

Eligibility:

The call is open to scholars (both on junior and senior levels) who have been awarded their doctoral degree at least three months before the start of the fellowship.

Individual residential fellowships will allow researchers to conduct a project of their own choice, connected to MIASA’s thematic research areas. Projects can be at conceptional stage, mid-term phase or final stage (analyzing data, writing up findings). Fellowships are residential with only shorter absences possible and with only limited funds to support activities such as field work trips. The selection is made by MIASA’s distinguished international Academic Advisory Board. In a strictly merit-based selection process, the individual fellowships are awarded to researchers of top academic quality with an innovative and high-quality research topic. The all-important selection criteria are the academic excellence of the applicant and the fellowship proposal. MIASA is committed to inclusion, gender equality, and family friendliness. The MIASA fellowship program thus aims for gender parity and promotes affirmative action policies.

Benefits: The successful applicants become MIASA fellows with all the corresponding rights and obligations for the requested funding period. For fellows affiliated with a home institution the fellows’ salary or teaching substitution costs are met by MIASA for every full fellowship month on the principle of “no loss, no gain,” and paid directly to his/her home institution. In cases where this is not possible an individual grant based on the candidate’s salary at his/her home institution can be offered. Fellows may be eligible for a post adjustment to compensate for the difference in the cost of living based on a case-by-case justification. Fellows without employment receive an individual monthly grant. For fellows from outside Accra, MIASA provides accommodation (or an equivalent accommodation allowance of up to 1500€/month) and reimburses travel costs. In addition, a contribution to support research undertaken at MIASA can be granted to all MIASA fellows upon application to MIASA directors (max. 250€ per fellow per month). MIASA fellows who come with family members to Accra can receive a family allowance. Fellowships are funded by the German Federal Ministry for Education and Research via the University of Freiburg/FRIAS.

The Institute provides its fellows with office space on the University of Ghana campus. Fellows have full access to all library services at the University of Ghana and, electronically, at the University of Freiburg, Germany. For fellows from francophone and lusophone Africa MIASA can offer funding for courses in advanced academic English during the fellowship at the University of Ghana. A full-time presence of fellows at MIASA for the entire fellowship period is required. Periods of leave need to be negotiated with the MIASA directors prior to the signing of the fellowship agreement, and must not exceed a total of more than 1/6 of the fellowship duration.

Duration of Award: 3 to 12 months duration within the period between 1st of June and 31st of August.

How to Apply:

Applications will be accepted in English and French. The completed application form together with the information indicated below have to be uploaded on the application webpage (here). After submission of the documents, applicants receive an acknowledgement of receipt providing contact details and including a copy of their submission. Incomplete or late applications will not be considered.

Information on the application and selection process (required documents, eligibility criteria, evaluation criteria, timeline and stages of the selection process) is provided in the Application Guidelines for Individual Fellowships.

Kindly click on the link below to apply:

https://www.ug.edu.gh/mias-africa/open-calls

TITLE: Dartmouth Neukom Postdoctoral Fellows Program 2027: $70,000 Fellowship for Interdisciplinary Researchers in Computation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Neukom Institute at Dartmouth College has announced the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellows Competition 2027, an exceptional opportunity for recent PhD graduates and emerging scholars whose research crosses traditional academic boundaries and incorporates computation as a significant intellectual, methodological, or practical component.

The prestigious fellowship is designed for highly motivated interdisciplinary researchers who are interested in exploring complex questions that cannot easily be confined to a single academic discipline. Successful candidates will receive the opportunity to conduct independent research at Dartmouth College while working across departments, collaborating with faculty mentors, teaching seminars, and becoming part of a vibrant intellectual community focused on computational thinking and interdisciplinary scholarship.

The Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship positions are scheduled to begin on September 1, 2027. Selected Fellows will receive appointments lasting two years, with the possibility of requesting a third year. For the 2027–2028 academic year, Neukom Fellows will receive a stipend of $70,000, alongside additional financial support for equipment, travel, and research materials.

The competition provides an important platform for scholars whose work sits at the intersection of disciplines and computation. Whether computation serves as a methodological tool, a conceptual framework, or an explicit component of a research project, the fellowship encourages innovative approaches that challenge conventional academic boundaries.

About the Dartmouth Neukom Institute Postdoctoral Fellows Program

The Neukom Institute at Dartmouth College supports research and intellectual exploration at the intersection of computation and multiple academic disciplines. Its Postdoctoral Fellows Program brings together scholars whose work demonstrates the potential to bridge fields, develop new approaches to research, and expand how computational ideas can contribute to the understanding of complex problems.

The fellowship is particularly suited to researchers who do not fit neatly into traditional academic categories. Applicants may come from disciplines across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, arts, engineering, and other fields, provided they can demonstrate a meaningful connection between their research interests and the broader theme of computation.

A central feature of the Neukom Fellowship is its interdisciplinary structure. Fellows are expected to engage with faculty members and academic departments across Dartmouth College rather than working exclusively within a single disciplinary environment.

The program seeks individuals who can demonstrate both:

A history of successful collaboration across disciplinary boundaries; and

Strong evidence of independence, initiative, and the ability to develop original research ideas.

This balance between collaboration and independent scholarship makes the fellowship particularly attractive to researchers seeking to establish themselves as leaders in emerging interdisciplinary fields.

Why the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship Is Unique

Many postdoctoral opportunities are structured around a specific department, laboratory, or narrowly defined research area. The Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship takes a broader approach by encouraging scholars to connect different academic perspectives through computational research and thinking.

Successful Fellows will have the opportunity to:

Conduct independent interdisciplinary research.

Work with faculty members from two Dartmouth College departments.

Develop relationships across multiple academic disciplines.

Explore innovative research questions.

Engage with computational concepts and methodologies.

Teach one seminar course each year.

Access financial support for research activities.

Participate in Dartmouth’s academic and intellectual community.

Build professional networks with scholars across different disciplines.

Develop new approaches that move beyond conventional academic paradigms.

The program recognizes that some of the most important contemporary research challenges require perspectives from multiple disciplines. By supporting scholars who can work across these boundaries, the Neukom Institute aims to encourage new forms of intellectual collaboration and discovery.

Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship Funding and Financial Benefits

One of the major advantages of the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship is the financial support provided to selected candidates.

For the 2027–2028 academic year, Neukom Fellows will receive a stipend of:

$70,000

In addition to the annual stipend, Fellows can access additional funding for important research-related needs.

Additional support may be available for:

Research equipment.

Academic travel.

Conference participation.

Research materials.

Other resources necessary to support the Fellow’s scholarly work.

This financial structure allows Fellows to focus significantly on their research and professional development while receiving institutional support for activities that contribute to their academic projects.

The fellowship appointment is initially structured as a two-year position, providing researchers with substantial time to develop and advance an interdisciplinary research agenda. Fellows may also have the option to request a third year, depending on program arrangements and individual circumstances.

Fellowship Structure and Academic Experience

The Neukom Fellows Program provides more than financial support. It offers a comprehensive academic environment designed to help emerging scholars expand their research networks and intellectual perspectives.

1. Two-Year Fellowship Appointment

Selected candidates will receive appointments lasting two years. This extended period gives Fellows the opportunity to undertake substantial research projects rather than focusing only on short-term academic activities.

The possibility of requesting a third year may provide additional flexibility for scholars whose research requires further development.

2. Mentorship Across Two Departments

One of the defining features of the program is interdisciplinary mentorship.

Neukom Fellows will be mentored by faculty members representing two different departments at Dartmouth College. This structure encourages Fellows to actively engage with different intellectual traditions and methodologies.

Working across departments can help researchers:

Develop broader perspectives.

Establish collaborations outside their original discipline.

Access different methodological approaches.

Test research ideas with diverse academic audiences.

Build interdisciplinary professional networks.

Develop innovative approaches to complex research questions.

3. Departmental Residence

While Fellows will work across two academic departments, they will take up residence in one department at Dartmouth College.

This arrangement provides Fellows with an academic home while simultaneously allowing them to maintain meaningful engagement with another disciplinary environment.

4. Teaching Opportunity

Neukom Fellows will teach one seminar course each year on a subject related to their interests and expertise.

This teaching component provides an opportunity for Fellows to:

Develop university-level teaching experience.

Design an original seminar.

Share their research interests with students.

Explore interdisciplinary topics in a classroom setting.

Strengthen their academic portfolio.

Gain valuable experience for future faculty and research positions.

5. Focus on Research

Apart from the teaching seminar, Fellows do not have additional duties specified by the program.

This allows successful candidates to devote substantial attention to their research projects, collaborations, and scholarly development.

Research Focus: Computation and Interdisciplinary Scholarship

A central requirement of the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship is a meaningful connection between an applicant’s research and the theme of computation.

Importantly, computation does not necessarily have to be interpreted narrowly.

According to the program description, computation may serve as:

A framing concept for intellectual exploration.

An explicit methodological component of research.

A tool for investigating complex questions.

A foundation for interdisciplinary collaboration.

A means of connecting different academic fields.

This broad approach makes the fellowship relevant to researchers working in a wide range of disciplines.

For example, applicants may explore intersections between computation and areas such as:

Computer science.

Artificial intelligence.

Data science.

Digital humanities.

Computational social science.

Mathematics.

Engineering.

Biology.

Environmental studies.

Economics.

Philosophy.

Linguistics.

Media studies.

Creative arts.

Public policy.

History.

Literature.

Psychology.

Physics.

Education.

Communication studies.

Cultural studies.

The specific research area does not need to belong exclusively to a computational discipline. However, applicants must clearly demonstrate how computation meaningfully intersects with their proposed work.

Eligibility Requirements for the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship 2027

The Neukom Institute welcomes applications from scholars across different academic backgrounds.

To be eligible for the fellowship, applicants should meet the following requirements.

Academic Qualification

Applicants must hold or expect to receive one of the following qualifications by September 2027:

PhD in any discipline.

Doctor of Musical Arts (DMA).

Master of Fine Arts (MFA), where applicable to the fellowship requirements.

The program specifically indicates that candidates may be expected to complete their doctoral qualification by September 2027.

This makes the fellowship particularly relevant for:

Recent PhD graduates.

Final-stage doctoral candidates.

Emerging scholars preparing to transition into postdoctoral research.

Researchers seeking an interdisciplinary academic environment after completing their doctoral studies.

Research Connection to Computation

Applicants must demonstrate research interests that strongly intersect with the broader theme of computation.

Candidates should clearly explain:

How computation relates to their research.

How computational ideas, methods, or frameworks contribute to their work.

Why interdisciplinary collaboration is important for their proposed research.

How the fellowship environment would strengthen their intellectual development.

Interest in Multidisciplinary Research

The Neukom Institute is specifically looking for scholars who are interested in working beyond traditional disciplinary boundaries.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate:

Experience collaborating across disciplines.

Interest in multidisciplinary research.

Openness to different academic perspectives.

Ability to communicate with researchers from different fields.

Willingness to explore new methodologies and intellectual frameworks.

Independent Thinking and Initiative

Although collaboration is important, successful applicants must also demonstrate independence.

The program seeks candidates with evidence of:

Original thinking.

Research initiative.

Intellectual independence.

Leadership potential.

The ability to develop and pursue innovative research questions.

Ability to Think Beyond Traditional Paradigms

The fellowship strongly emphasizes innovative and unconventional thinking.

Applicants should demonstrate the capacity to:

Challenge traditional academic boundaries.

Connect ideas from different disciplines.

Develop creative research methodologies.

Explore emerging questions.

Think critically about established assumptions.

Build new intellectual frameworks.

Required Application Materials

Applicants for the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellows Program must prepare several important documents.

Candidates are encouraged to begin preparing their applications early, particularly because identifying and contacting potential Dartmouth faculty mentors may require significant research and communication.

The required application materials include the following.

1. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a comprehensive academic curriculum vitae.

The CV should clearly highlight relevant experience, including:

Academic qualifications.

Research experience.

Publications.

Academic appointments.

Teaching experience.

Research collaborations.

Conferences and presentations.

Awards and honors.

Technical or methodological skills.

Interdisciplinary projects.

Candidates should ensure that their CV clearly demonstrates their academic development and capacity to contribute to an interdisciplinary research environment.

2. Publications List

Applicants are required to provide a list of publications.

This may include:

Journal articles.

Book chapters.

Books.

Conference papers.

Working papers.

Research reports.

Other relevant scholarly publications.

Where appropriate, candidates should clearly identify publications that demonstrate interdisciplinary or computational aspects of their work.

3. Statement of Research Interests

Applicants must submit a statement of research interests with a maximum length of two pages.

The statement should include a short description of the research the applicant would like to pursue as a Neukom Fellow.

A strong research statement should clearly address:

The central research question.

The importance of the proposed research.

The relationship between the project and computation.

The interdisciplinary nature of the work.

The proposed methodology.

Expected research outcomes.

Potential academic or societal contributions.

Why Dartmouth College provides an appropriate environment for the research.

Because the fellowship is highly interdisciplinary, applicants should ensure that their research statement is understandable to readers from multiple academic backgrounds.

4. Proposed Departments and Faculty Mentors

Applicants must describe:

Which Dartmouth College departments they are interested in working with.

Which Dartmouth faculty members they would like to collaborate with.

Why these academic connections are relevant to their proposed research.

How working across multiple departments would enhance their scholarship.

The Neukom Institute strongly encourages applicants to research Dartmouth’s departments and faculty listings when preparing this section.

Candidates are also strongly encouraged to identify potential faculty mentors and contact them while developing their applications.

This is an important part of the application strategy because demonstrating a clear understanding of Dartmouth’s academic environment can strengthen the connection between the applicant’s proposed research and the fellowship.

Applicants should therefore consider:

Identifying departments relevant to their research.

Reviewing faculty profiles.

Reading about faculty research interests.

Identifying potential interdisciplinary connections.

Contacting prospective mentors where appropriate.

Explaining clearly how those academic relationships could support the proposed research.

5. Three Referees and Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must provide details for three referees.

The letters of recommendation should speak directly to the aims and objectives of the fellowship.

Applicants will provide the referees’ email addresses through the application system. Referees will then receive an email with access to upload their letters directly.

Applicants will not have access to the submitted recommendation letters.

Candidates should carefully select referees who can discuss areas such as:

Research ability.

Academic independence.

Interdisciplinary experience.

Collaborative skills.

Intellectual creativity.

Leadership potential.

Ability to develop innovative research.

Suitability for a postdoctoral academic environment.

Although applicants are encouraged to have their applications completed by the main deadline, referees have an additional period to submit their letters.

6. Optional Writing Sample or Creative Work

Applicants may optionally submit one paper written in English.

The work may be:

Published; or

Unpublished.

Applicants whose work involves creative practice may submit comparable creative work instead.

A strong optional submission could provide additional evidence of:

Research quality.

Writing ability.

Originality.

Methodological expertise.

Interdisciplinary thinking.

7. Optional Teaching Statement

Applicants may also submit a teaching statement.

This can be particularly useful for candidates who want to demonstrate their readiness to teach the required annual seminar.

A teaching statement may discuss:

Teaching philosophy.

Previous teaching experience.

Approaches to interdisciplinary education.

Student engagement strategies.

Proposed seminar ideas.

8. Optional Cover Letter

Candidates may submit an optional cover letter.

A well-written cover letter could briefly summarize:

Academic background.

Research interests.

Interdisciplinary experience.

Connection to computation.

Motivation for applying.

Why the Neukom Fellowship is an appropriate next step.

Importance of Contacting Potential Dartmouth Mentors

One of the strongest recommendations provided by the program is that applicants should actively identify and contact prospective mentors at Dartmouth College.

Candidates are encouraged to begin making these academic connections while drafting their applications.

This approach can be valuable because it allows applicants to:

Better understand Dartmouth’s research environment.

Identify faculty whose expertise aligns with their work.

Develop stronger interdisciplinary research proposals.

Explain why specific departments are relevant.

Demonstrate genuine interest in collaboration.

Clarify how their proposed research could fit within Dartmouth’s academic community.

Applicants should approach potential mentors professionally and thoughtfully.

Before contacting a faculty member, candidates should:

Carefully review the faculty member’s research profile.

Understand their major research interests.

Identify a genuine connection with their own work.

Prepare a concise introduction.

Briefly explain the proposed research idea.

Explain why the faculty member’s expertise is relevant.

Avoid sending generic messages to multiple academics.

Early preparation is particularly important because identifying appropriate mentors and developing meaningful academic connections may take time.

Residence Requirement

Neukom Fellows are generally expected to be in residence at Dartmouth College.

The primary exception relates to travel associated with:

Research activities.

Academic conferences.

Other approved scholarly engagements.

Candidates should therefore be prepared to participate actively in Dartmouth’s academic community during the fellowship period.

Being in residence provides Fellows with opportunities to:

Meet regularly with faculty mentors.

Participate in academic discussions.

Collaborate with researchers.

Engage with students.

Attend seminars and events.

Build interdisciplinary networks.

Important Dates and Application Timeline

Applicants should pay close attention to the official competition schedule.

Application Site Opens

August 1, 2026

The online application system becomes available through Interfolio.

Application Deadline

December 1, 2026

Applicants should submit their complete applications by this date.

The program indicates that application review will begin on December 1, 2026.

Letters of Recommendation Deadline

December 8, 2026

Letters of recommendation must be submitted no later than this date.

Applicants should contact their referees well in advance to ensure they have sufficient time to prepare strong recommendation letters.

Fellowship Start Date

September 1, 2027

Successful Neukom Postdoctoral Fellows are expected to begin their appointments.

How to Apply for the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship 2027

The application process is completed online through the Interfolio application platform.

Interested candidates should follow these general steps.

Step 1: Review the Fellowship Requirements

Carefully read all eligibility criteria and application requirements before beginning the application.

Ensure that your academic qualifications and research interests align with the program.

Step 2: Develop Your Research Proposal

Prepare a strong research statement explaining:

Your proposed research.

Its interdisciplinary nature.

Its connection to computation.

Why the research is important.

How Dartmouth College would support the project.

Step 3: Identify Relevant Dartmouth Departments

Explore Dartmouth College’s academic departments and identify those connected to your research interests.

Consider how different departments could contribute complementary perspectives to your project.

Step 4: Identify Potential Faculty Mentors

Review Dartmouth faculty profiles and identify scholars whose research aligns with your proposed work.

The program strongly encourages applicants to explore potential academic connections while preparing their applications.

Step 5: Contact Potential Mentors

Where appropriate, reach out professionally to prospective mentors.

Explain your research interests and your interest in the interdisciplinary environment provided by the Neukom Fellowship.

Step 6: Prepare Your Supporting Documents

Compile the required materials, including:

Curriculum vitae.

Publications list.

Two-page research statement.

Description of relevant departments and faculty mentors.

Referee information.

Consider including optional materials where they strengthen your application.

Step 7: Notify Your Referees Early

Contact your three referees well before the deadline.

Provide them with:

Information about the fellowship.

Your research proposal.

Your CV.

Relevant application deadlines.

This will help them prepare letters that are specifically tailored to the aims of the Neukom Fellowship.

Step 8: Submit Your Application Online

Applications can be submitted through Interfolio once the application system opens.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day, as early submission provides time to address any technical issues.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

The Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship is designed for ambitious scholars working at the intersection of disciplines. Applicants should therefore ensure that their applications clearly communicate both academic depth and interdisciplinary vision.

Clearly Explain the Computational Connection

Do not assume that reviewers will automatically understand how your research relates to computation.

Clearly explain whether computation functions as:

A research methodology.

A theoretical framework.

A conceptual lens.

A practical tool.

A core component of your proposed project.

Demonstrate Genuine Interdisciplinarity

Simply mentioning multiple disciplines may not be sufficient.

Applicants should demonstrate how different fields will actively contribute to the proposed research.

Explain:

What each discipline contributes.

Why one discipline alone is insufficient.

How interdisciplinary collaboration will create new insights.

Balance Collaboration and Independence

The fellowship seeks candidates who can collaborate effectively while also pursuing independent scholarship.

Use examples from your academic experience to demonstrate both qualities.

Research Dartmouth Thoroughly

A strong application should demonstrate why Dartmouth College is particularly suitable for the proposed project.

Avoid generic statements.

Instead, identify:

Relevant departments.

Potential faculty collaborators.

Academic resources.

Interdisciplinary opportunities.

Select Referees Strategically

Choose referees who understand your research trajectory and can provide detailed examples of your abilities.

Ideally, recommendation letters should reinforce the themes emphasized throughout the application.

Begin Preparation Early

Because the application involves:

Developing a research proposal.

Identifying multiple departments.

Researching Dartmouth faculty.

Contacting potential mentors.

Coordinating recommendation letters.

Applicants should begin preparing well before the December deadline.

Diversity and Equal Opportunity

Dartmouth College states that it is an equal opportunity and affirmative action employer with a strong commitment to diversity.

The institution encourages applications from a broad spectrum of individuals, including:

Women.

Persons of color.

Persons with disabilities.

Veterans.

Other legally protected groups.

This commitment reflects the Neukom Institute’s interest in building a diverse intellectual community that brings together different perspectives, experiences, academic backgrounds, and approaches to research.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship may be particularly suitable for scholars who answer yes to several of the following questions:

Are you completing a PhD or recently completed doctoral research?

Does your work intersect meaningfully with computation?

Does your research cross traditional academic boundaries?

Are you interested in working with scholars from multiple disciplines?

Do you have an innovative research idea that requires diverse academic perspectives?

Are you comfortable developing independent research projects?

Do you want postdoctoral teaching experience?

Are you interested in becoming part of an interdisciplinary academic community?

Can you identify Dartmouth faculty members whose expertise could strengthen your research?

If these characteristics align with your academic goals, the Neukom Fellowship could provide an important opportunity to develop an innovative research agenda.

Key Benefits of the Dartmouth Neukom Postdoctoral Fellowship

Successful Fellows can benefit from a combination of financial support, research opportunities, mentorship, teaching experience, and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Key benefits include:

A $70,000 stipend for 2027–2028.

A two-year fellowship appointment.

The possibility of requesting a third year.

Additional support for equipment.

Funding support for research travel.

Support for research materials.

Mentorship from faculty in two Dartmouth departments.

An opportunity to conduct interdisciplinary research.

Residence within Dartmouth College’s academic community.

The opportunity to teach one seminar course per year.

No additional duties beyond the specified fellowship responsibilities.

Opportunities to collaborate across traditional academic boundaries.

Access to an intellectually diverse research environment.

Professional development through research and teaching.

Opportunities to expand academic networks.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the Neukom Postdoctoral Fellows Competition 2027 is: December 1, 2026

Applicants should note that letters of recommendation are due no later than: December 8, 2026

The application portal opens on August 1, 2026, and selected Fellows are expected to begin their appointments on September 1, 2027.

APPLY HERE

How to Access the Official Application

Interested applicants should submit their applications online through the Interfolio application platform after the application portal opens.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Dartmouth Neukom Postdoctoral Fellows Program 2027.

Conclusion

The Dartmouth Neukom Postdoctoral Fellows Program 2027 represents an outstanding opportunity for emerging scholars whose work challenges traditional disciplinary boundaries and engages meaningfully with the broad field of computation. With a $70,000 stipend, additional research support, mentorship across two academic departments, teaching opportunities, and a two-year appointment with the potential for extension, the fellowship provides an exceptional environment for developing ambitious interdisciplinary research.

The program is particularly attractive because it welcomes researchers from diverse academic disciplines rather than restricting participation to a single field. Candidates who can demonstrate a strong connection between their research and computation, an interest in multidisciplinary collaboration, and the ability to think independently and creatively are encouraged to consider applying.

Prospective applicants should begin preparing early by refining their research ideas, identifying relevant Dartmouth departments, connecting with potential faculty mentors, and securing strong recommendation letters. Given the fellowship’s emphasis on innovative scholarship and interdisciplinary collaboration, a carefully developed application that clearly communicates both intellectual originality and the value of cross-disciplinary research could significantly strengthen a candidate’s prospects.

With applications closing on December 1, 2026, eligible researchers have an opportunity to position themselves for a transformative postdoctoral experience at one of the leading institutions supporting interdisciplinary research at the intersection of computation and the wider academic world.

TITLE: Press Release: A Free Open-Source Digital Grants Management System Developed for Science Granting Councils in Sub-Saharan Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana and Nairobi, Kenya (October 12, 2021) – A digital grants management system has been developed and positioned for adoption by Africa’s Science Granting Councils. This forms part of activities being implemented by the Research Management Project under the Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI).

The Research Management Project of SGCI, seeks to strengthen the capacities of Africa’s Science Granting Councils to play their essential roles in research, knowledge generation and innovation through training, technical support, and peer-to-peer learning.

In an increasingly digitalized world, the development of the online system is critical and aims at improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the SGCs’ grants management processes. The partners involved – the Association of African Universities (AAU), the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST) developed the system as part of activities outlined in a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed by the parties.

The AAU, AAS and UNCST undertook to upgrade the UNCST grants management system and strategically position it for adoption by all the 15 SGCs participating in the SGCI. These are the Science Granting councils in Ghana, Burkina Faso, Cote d’Ivoire, Senegal, Botswana, Malawi, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Ethiopia, Namibia, and Rwanda.

Working collaboratively with the Councils, the system development partners ensured that the online grants management system is well equipped with multi-lingual functionalities and the flexibility to accommodate the different needs of the SGCs.

“To promote quick adoption of the system, an engagement process with key stakeholders and the SGCs has been carefully executed by the partners to ensure clarity concerning the differences that exist amongst the SGCs in terms of managing granting processes” said Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director of ICT, Communications and Knowledge Management at the AAU.

In ensuring that all requirements were met for the different groups of stakeholders who will be utilizing the system, the team put together for its development comprised of Project Management and Oversight; Grants Management Experts; Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Experts; Systems Engineering and Software Development Experts; as well as Finance and Audit personnel.

“The team was cognizant of the need to promote standardized processes among all the SGCs while preserving requirements for the grants management processes of the individual SGCs” she added.

The digitalized grants management system broadly encompasses functions such as Calls for Proposals (publication and receipt of applications); Reviewers Database Management; Proposals Completeness Check and Criteria Establishment; Technical Review of Proposals and Criteria Establishment; Grants Awarding and Contracting; Grants Monitoring, Progress Reporting, Evaluation, and Learning. Other functions include Financial Management and Monitoring; Rolling out and implementation of the system; Knowledge Transfer and Continuous improvement of the Grant Management System.

The implementation of the digital grants management system by the SGCs will contribute towards integrated national data systems and facilitate the flow of data among diverse users and stakeholders.

The SGCI is a multi-funder initiative that is funded by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida), United Kingdom’s Department for International Development (DFID), Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC), South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF) and the German Research Foundation (DFG).

The Association of African Universities, the African Academy of Sciences and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST) are strongly committed to working closely with the Science Granting Councils to ensure full adoption of the system and optimum derivation of the benefits therein.

A copy of the Press Release can be downloaded from here – https://blog.aau.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Press-Release-_Digital-Grants-Managment-System_-SGCI-Research-Management-Project.pdf

TITLE: ACEPHAP Wins Over US$ 500,000 E-MOTIVE Research Project Grant

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Africa Centre of Excellence for Population Health and Policy (ACEPHAP) hosted by the Bayero University, Kano has recently obtained a grant of $553,054.86 from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation to conduct E-MOTIVE trial in collaboration with University of Birmingham, United Kingdom.

The Director of the Centre, Professor Hadiza Galadanci revealed this when she led the Management team of the Centre on a congratulatory visit to the newly appointed Vice Chancellor of Bayero University, Kano, Professor Sagir Adamu Abbas.

She explained that the E-MOTIVE trial which stands for “ Early detection of postpartum hemorrhage and treatment using the World Health Organization MOTIVE First response bundle: a cluster randomized trial with health economic analysis and mixed methods evaluation, is aimed at preventing maternal deaths by implementing the World Health Organization (WHO) prevention and treatment guideline for Postpartum Hemorrhage. It is being implemented in five countries of Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, and Sri Lanka.

Professor Galadanci also disclosed that 16 health facilities across Nigeria have been selected for the research project, with ACEPHAP coordinating the Project in Nigeria. She further stated other achievements of the Center including the commencement of five MSc programmes across the seven collaborating Departments of Biochemistry, Nursing, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Community Medicine, Paediatrics, Internal Medicine and Psychiatry. She added that, the centre has enrolled 50 students with 14 regional students from Kenya, Cameroun, Niger Republic, Sierra Leone, Liberia and Senegal, etc.

She further revealed that the Centre is developing a Moodle e-learning management system in collaboration with the University’s Centre for Information Technology which she said would be useful even beyond COVID-19. Currently, with the support of the World Bank, Association of African Universities (AAU) and Coursera, students will be taking free courses on the Coursera platform.

Professor Galadanci also stated that ACEPHAP in collaboration with World Health Organization (WHO) had recently concluded a research to evaluate the usability of the Revised Partograph or Labour Care Guide (LCG), adding that maternal health care providers (nurses/midwives and doctors) from Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital and Muhammad Abdullahi Wase Hospital all in Kano, Nigeria were trained as part of the evaluation project.

The Vice Chancellor, Professor Sagir Adamu Abbas commended the ACEPHAP team for the successes recorded so far by the Centre within its core mandates of research and postgraduate training. He said the level of successes recorded within the shortest time of the Centre’s existence gladdens all members of the Bayero University family. Again, he reiterated the University’s total commitment to support the centre at all times to achieve its goals and objectives.

The African Centre of Excellence for Population Health and Policy (ACEPHAP) is one of the World Bank supported Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) aimed at strengthening interdisciplinary approaches to promote population health outcome through training and research for evidence-informed policy development in Africa.

TITLE: Workshop on Strategic Foresight and Strategic Intelligence for Leaders, Managers, Academics and Administrators in Higher Education Institutions in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU), a Pan-African Higher Education organization, invites stakeholders to participate in an upcoming training program being organized on Strategic Foresight and Strategic Intelligence in Africa with the following details:

Workshop Title: Strategic Foresight and Strategic Intelligence for Leaders, Managers, Academics and Administrators in Higher Education Institutions in Africa

Date: 8th -11th October 2024

Venue: Association of African Universities Secretariat, Accra, Ghana

Target Participants: The workshop is recommended for Academics, Leaders, Librarians, Registrars, Administrators, University Management, Heads of Resource Mobilization & Partnership Development in institutions, Executive Directors, Directors, Program Coordinators, Staff of International Relations Offices, Finance and Budgeting Managers, Project Managers and Officers, Staff Responsible for Resource Development, Partnership & Policy Managers, and Planning Officers.

Registration Link: https://forms.office.com/r/yvY1z52mVJ

Registration Fee: The registration fees for the 4-day event are as follows:

AAU Member Institutions – $700

Non – AAU Member Institutions – $800

This will cover workshop attendance fees, snacks and lunches, training materials, certificates, and other logistics.

Overall Objective of the Workshop

This workshop aims to create future-ready and alert African higher education institutions that can adapt as the future evolves (anticipation, awareness, agility, and capability). This four-day practical capacity-building workshop focuses on foresight for strategic decision-making in higher education institutional contexts and helps participants understand and deal with the complexity underlying the operations of universities and research institutions. Participants will gain hands-on experience in applying strategic foresight tools (e.g., STEEP driver mapping, futures wheel, visioning, backcasting, wind tunneling, three horizons, archetypes, and roadmap) and working in groups. Participants will apply theoretical perspectives from cognitive and social psychology, decision theory, economics, organizational behavior, political science, or other behavioral science disciplines.

Specific Objectives

The training workshop is intended to help participants:

Expand their thinking beyond the present and/or near-term future.

Consider the long-term implications of current assumptions, decisions, and courses of action.

Think backward in time to better anticipate how the situation may evolve in the future.

Think holistically about multiple factors and their interactions to anticipate potential second-and third-order effects.

Develop a system thinking mindset and the skills and tools to apply that mindset to complex challenges and management problems for decision-makers in higher education institutions in Africa.

Critically evaluate the complexity of grand challenges in higher education and systematically address them.

Use strategic foresight for effective strategic planning in the context of the SDGs –building vision, resilience, and capability.

Delivery Mode

The workshop will be face-to-face, hands-on, and interactive through a combination of lecture, discussion, and group work. The workshop will give participants a structured approach to developing and implementing strategic foresight. The approach is proven and incorporates tools and techniques to aid analysis, the creation of options, and the evaluation of alternatives. Participants will learn to use one of the most compelling strategic foresight methodologies in use today, The Actionable Futures Toolkit and the Horizons Strategic Foresight Approach.

Expected Outcomes

On completing the workshop, participants will be able to:

Characterise grand challenges in higher education in Africa and delineate the potential of strategic foresight in addressing them.

Apply strategic foresight to institutional challenges and societal problems to identify leverage points for transformative change.

Critically reflect upon the strengths and limitations of strategic foresight to solve complex problems in higher education, and society, at large.

About our facilitators

Our facilitators are distinguished experts in the field of strategic foresight and strategic intelligence, with many years of experience in higher education. They have dedicated their careers to advancing strategic thinking and intelligence among leaders and managers in academia. These are:

Professor Tobias De Coning, Dean and Chair, Department of Innovation, and Entrepreneurship, ISM, Paris

Professor Frederick Ato Armah, Director of Research and Programmes (DRAP), Association of African Universities

TITLE: AAU e-Learning SUMMIT 2026: IDENTIFYING THE PRIORITIES THAT WILL SHAPE THE FUTURE OF DIGITAL EDUCATION IN AFRICA

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Press Release – Accra, Ghana, March 11, 2026 – The Association of African Universities (AAU) is pleased to announce the 2026 e-Learning Summit, scheduled to take place virtually on Wednesday, April 15, 2026, at 1 PM GMT / 3 PM SAST. Click to register here – https://forms.office.com/r/TQyh40nAd9

Building on the success of the 2024 and 2025 editions, this year’s summit adopts the theme “e-Learning Priorities for African Universities,” a deliberate shift inward to ask a fundamental question: What are the real, actionable e-learning priorities for African universities today and in the near future?

The Summit will bring together higher education leaders, policymakers, instructional designers, and industry experts from across the continent to engage in critical dialogue on shaping the future of digital education in Africa. The programme will explore key thematic areas including infrastructure and access, quality assurance and innovative pedagogy, and digital skills development aligned with workforce needs.

Participants will engage in interactive panel discussions, case study presentations, and collaborative dialogue sessions covering strategies for bridging the digital divide, enhancing programme quality, integrating AI in teaching and learning, and aligning curricula with evolving workforce demands.

A core outcome of the summit will be a consolidated report documenting the key e-learning priorities identified by African universities, along with a collection of practical case studies and best practices from diverse institutions made available to all AAU members. Click to register here – https://forms.office.com/r/TQyh40nAd9

The summit addresses the urgent need for African universities to articulate and act on their e-learning priorities in the face of rapid technological change. By providing a platform for surfacing institutional challenges, facilitating peer learning, and identifying systemic gaps, the programme aims to produce tangible outcomes, including:

Enhanced networking and collaboration among universities, policymakers, and private sector actors.

Increased awareness of resources, partnerships, and support available through AAU and its partners.

A clear roadmap for continental collaboration and targeted support for member institutions.

This integrated summit represents a critical step in ensuring that e-learning across Africa is aligned with the specific priorities of its universities, improving access and equity, enhancing quality and relevance, building institutional capacity, fostering regional collaboration, and leveraging technology, including AI, to improve pedagogy and learner support.

Registration

Participation in the summit is free for AAU member institutions and interested stakeholders. To register, click here – https://forms.office.com/r/TQyh40nAd9

About the AAU

The Association of African Universities is an international, non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African universities to promote cooperation among institutions on the continent and strengthen their engagement with the global academic community. Founded in 1967, the AAU serves as the voice of higher education in Africa. Its mission is to enhance the quality, relevance, and sustainability of African higher education by supporting institutional development, fostering collaboration, and promoting innovation across the continent.

TITLE: Continental Workshop for Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
CONTINENTAL WORKSHOP FOR DIRECTORS OF ICT / CHIEF INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY OFFICERS

INTRODUCTION

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is a membership-based network of 425 plus universities covering the 5 regions of Africa and its mission is to enhance the quality and relevance of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development. Since 1967 the AAU has been the leading advocate for higher education in Africa, demonstrating the capacity to provide support for its member institutions in meeting their national, continental, and global needs.

As part of creating value for its members the AAU regularly runs various capacity building programs for the benefit of various thematic groups within the member universities. These capacity building programs offer discounted fees to staff from the member universities to demonstrate the value of their loyal membership to the AAU.

The AAU also hosts various diverse forums for exchanges, discussions, engagements, collaborations, and advocacy for the purpose of fulfilling its mission and to improve the functions of its member universities. The AAU has created the Africa Research, Innovation and Development Network (AFRID) to promote the establishment of thematic networks representing the diverse functions and research interests of member universities, individual researchers, and individual administrative staff.

WHY THE WORKSHOP

The continental workshop for Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers will be hosted by the AAU for the purpose of strengthening collaborations among the Africa-wide Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers (DICT/CITOs). The workshop also aims to build the capacities of DICT/CITOs in emerging areas of leadership and strategic management; IT governance; business acumen; technology trends and innovation; cybersecurity; data management and analytics; cloud computing; digital transformation; vendor management; regulatory compliance; communication and stakeholder management; project management; and personal and professional development.

The plans are that the continental workshop will be an annual gathering of DICT/CITOs modelled around the computer society summer/winter schools, higher education information technology South Africa (HEITSA) and EDUCAUSE. The purpose of the continental annual DICT/CITOs workshop will be to serve as a joint voice for the Africa-wide IT profession in African Universities. The annual workshop will promote best practices and standards through the sharing of expertise among participating DICT/CITOs. The long-term goal of the continental DICT/CITOs workshop will be to support the sustainable application of digital tools, platforms, and strategies to transform African Higher Education.

OBJECTIVES AND INTENDED OUTCOMES OF THE ANNUAL WORKSHOP

The initial objectives of the annual workshop for Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers are:

To develop strategies for guiding the integration and adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) by African Universities.

To develop strategies for developing and deploying AI Literacy training programs for universities.

To build capacities of DICT/CITOs in key emerging areas such as IT governance, cybersecurity, vendor management, ERP implementation, cloud computing and digital transformation.

To initiate strategies for monitoring ICT development in African Higher Education Institutions.

To deliberate on opportunities (and implement) for joint purchases of technology licenses and equipment to reduce the costs to individual universities.

The expected outcomes from the annual workshops include:

Strengthened collaboration and networking among DICT/CITOs in the African continent.

Developed action plans and strategies for guiding AAU Member Universities to harness the benefits from Artificial Intelligence and other emerging technologies.

A program developed for monitoring the development of ICT in African Universities through annual surveys.

Agreement on future focus areas of the continental workshops of DICT/CITOs.

WORKSHOP FACILITATORS

High profile, experienced and well-respected IT professionals and thought leaders from industry and academia will be identified to facilitate these workshops. The workshops will be organized in such a way that practical case studies are shared, current information is provided, and participants are guided in terms of post-workshop action planning.

TARGET PARTICIPANTS

These workshops are strictly for Senior Leaders in African Universities that are responsible for the running and management of the Information and Communication Technology role and related infrastructure and systems. The target participants are:

Directors of Information and Communication Technology

Chief Information Technology Officers

Deputy Vice Chancellors responsible for Information technology

Senior Project Management Officers responsible for high-level IT projects implementation

DATES AND VENUE FOR THE 2024 WORKSHOP

The inaugural workshop will be hosted from 27-29 February 2024 in Accra Ghana.

LANGUAGE OF THE WORKSHOPS

The workshops will be delivered in the 4 languages of the Association of African Universities – Arabic, English, French and Portuguese. Interpretation will be available in the 4 languages.

HOW TO PARTICIPATE

The participation fees for DICT/CITOs from AAU member universities in good standing are US$800 per participant and these include facilitation fees, workshop materials, interpretation services, excursion within Accra and lunches, and refreshments during the workshop days.

DICT/CITOs from non-AAU member universities and DICT/CITOs whose universities are in bad standing will pay US$1,000 per participant.

Participants are responsible for their airfares, accommodation, visas, and general upkeep.

Please register to participate via this link: https://forms.office.com/r/x35b0UvyDJ

Please pay for your participation from this online link: https://pay.aau.org/cwd-accra

CONTACT DETAILS

If you have any questions, please contact Miss Nodumo Dhlamini on ndhlamini@aau.org or call her on +233553019588. Please also copy Mr Abdul Manaf Sulemana on amsulemana@aau.org

DOWNLOAD THE WORKSHOP CONCEPT NOTES IN THE FOUR AAU LANGUAGES

Arabic: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/PKikYmTs9zRjgfL

English: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/zmt6oPG3xxyHjXZ

French: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/Ebos58JzXtnPR9s

Portuguese: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/opm786eZWmS4ey3

SELECTION OF MODULES TO BE COVERED

A) Leadership and Strategic Management of AI in African Higher Education by DICT/CITOs

The recent webinars organized by the AAU revealed a great need for DICT/CITOs to take fore-front leadership in supporting their universities to understand what opportunities and challenges are posed by Artificial Intelligence. DICT/CITOs should lead the discourse, strategy formulation and capacity building within their universities. This module will cover the following:

Change management, policies, and strategies for AI adoption.

Driving AI innovation within the university.

Evaluating and adopting AI technologies that align with your university goals.

Developing AI literacy training programs.

B) Information Technology Governance

IT governance is part of corporate governance, and its goal is to improve the overall management of information technology (IT) and generate improved value from investments made in information technology. IT governance frameworks help universities manage their IT risks effectively and ensure that the activities associated with information technology are aligned with their overall objectives. IT governance enables a university to demonstrate measurable results against the broader university’s strategies and goals; respond to relevant legal and regulatory obligations; assure higher education stakeholders that they can have confidence in the university’s IT services; and facilitate an increase in the return on IT investment. This module will cover the following topics:

Strategic alignment with the university’s objectives

Achieving value delivery and optimization

Risk management and mitigation

Performance measurement and monitoring

Resource management and optimization

C) Cybersecurity

In the quickly evolving digital landscape, Africa is experiencing significant advancements in technology adoption and connectivity. However, these advancements come with increased cybersecurity threats that can undermine the region’s progress. This module will discuss the challenges and solutions relevant to cybersecurity in African higher education institutions and will explore practical strategies to safeguard African HEI networks and promote a secure digital culture. The module will include:

The complexities of cybersecurity in African HEIs, including the challenges, solutions, and emerging trends.

Developing and implementing robust cybersecurity strategies.

Managing cyber risks and ensuring compliance with regulations.

Incident response and crisis management.

Cybersecurity advocacy, awareness campaigns, and capacity-building activities, and achieving the digital resilience of African HEIs.

D) Cloud Computing

African Universities are subscribing to various models of cloud computing infrastructure to host their digital management information systems, manage their email servers and other key resources. Cloud computing needs to be managed appropriately so that the university data and information are secure. This module will cover the following:

Cloud strategy development and implementation.

Cloud security and compliance.

Managing and optimizing cloud resources.

E) Communication and Stakeholder Management

The IT function is normally viewed as a technical function that works in the background to service the institution. Because of the growing importance of IT, it is now critical for DICT/CITOs to become proficient in communication and stakeholder management so that they obtain the buy-in and support for the digital transformation initiatives. This module will cover the following:

Effective communication with both technical and non-technical stakeholders.

Building relationships with other Senior Leaders in the university and elsewhere

Advocating for the IT department’s role in achieving business objectives.

F) ERP Implementation and digital transformation: lessons and pitfalls

African universities are investing significant financial and human resources in implementing university-wide enterprise resource planning digital systems. These ERPs focus on student information systems, financial management, library management, university hospitals management, dormitory management, and others. Some of the systems are developed in-house and others are purchased off the shelf. This module will cover the following:

Case studies of in-house developed ERPs

Case studies of off the shelf ERPs

Funding and sustaining ERP implementations.

Driving digital initiatives and transformations.

Integrating digital technologies into university business processes.

Enhancing university customer experiences through digital channels.

G) Strategies for monitoring ICT development in African Higher Education Institutions.

Data and information are critical for informing university top leadership and governments about the development of ICT in higher education institutions. When data is available the senior leaders can make informed decisions on how to support ICT development. This module will discuss the following:

Strategies for data collection about ICT development in African Universities

What data to collect

How to incentivize African universities to share ICT related data

H) Vendor Management and opportunities for joint purchases of technology licenses and equipment

Some of the potential benefits of speaking with one voice to vendors is the reduction of financial investments, better services, and standardization of services. This module will discuss the following:

Effective negotiation and relationship management with technology vendors.

Evaluating and selecting technology solutions.

Ensuring vendor compliance and performance.

Opportunities for continental level negotiations with technology vendors

I) Personal and Professional Development

Continuous learning and adaptability are crucial for Directors of ICT / Chief IT Officers to thrive in their roles, because of the quick pace of technological advancements and the evolving nature of higher education challenges. This module will cover the following topics

Continuous learning and staying abreast of industry trends.

Networking and participation in professional organizations.

Mentoring and coaching to develop the next generation of IT leaders.

J) Emerging Issues in ICT for Universities

This module will cover emerging issues, strategies, tools, and opportunities that benefit African higher education institutions. The module would also provide new information to Directors of ICT / Chief IT Officers so that they are most impactful in their roles.

TITLE: World Bank Small AI for Development Hackathon 2026: Build Inclusive AI Solutions and Win Sponsored Travel to Seoul

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the World Bank Group Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026, a global innovation opportunity inviting young people to develop practical artificial intelligence solutions for communities and economies facing limited connectivity, infrastructure and access to digital technology.

Participants will compete during a two-day hackathon on 3–4 October 2026, developing a working “Small AI” solution addressing a real development challenge in one of three sectors:

Health

Agriculture

Tourism

Three winning entries will be selected, with one winner representing each sector. The winners will be invited to present their solutions at the Global AI and Digital Summit 2026, taking place from 19–22 October 2026 in Seoul, Republic of Korea.

The final deadline to apply for the hackathon is 26 September 2026. Applications and all competition submissions must be completed in English.

Key Information at a Glance

Programme: Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026

Related event: Global AI and Digital Summit 2026

Hackathon dates: 3–4 October 2026

Hackathon format: Hybrid, with online participation and physical hubs

Application deadline: 26 September 2026

Summit dates: 19–22 October 2026

Summit location: Grand Hyatt, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Winner presentations: 21 October 2026

Challenge sectors: Health, agriculture and tourism

Application language: English

Team size: Individual applications or teams of up to four people

Number of World Bank challenge winners: Three

Competition partner: Hack-Nation

Referral code: WBGSmallAIGADS

Application form: Apply through the official Google Form

Official information: Global AI and Digital Summit 2026

The application form currently requires applicants to sign in to Google. Candidates should therefore ensure that they have access to an active Google account before starting.

About the Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge

The Small AI for Development Hackathon is organized by the World Bank Group’s Digital and AI Vice Presidency in collaboration with the World Bank Group Youth Summit, Development Economics Vice Presidency and Information and Technology Solutions.

Hack-Nation is responsible for managing the competition platform and administering the hackathon process. The World Bank Group serves as the sponsor and final judging authority.

The challenge is intended to encourage artificial intelligence development that responds to the actual conditions experienced in developing economies. Instead of assuming that every user has reliable broadband, an advanced smartphone and strong digital literacy, participants must consider environments where access to technology remains constrained.

The organizers are looking for solutions that can translate artificial intelligence into practical development outcomes rather than demonstrations of technology without a clearly defined problem or target user.

Why This Challenge Matters

The competition has been launched against the backdrop of significant global connectivity and employment challenges.

According to the official World Bank event page, more than two billion people remained offline as of 2025. At the same time, approximately 1.2 billion young people in the Global South are expected to reach working age during the coming decade, while current trends indicate that substantially fewer jobs will be created.

Artificial intelligence may support economic growth, better services and new employment opportunities. However, many existing AI applications have been designed for environments with advanced devices, dependable internet connectivity and users who already understand how to communicate with AI systems.

This challenge asks young innovators to reconsider those assumptions and create technology that can function under real development constraints.

What Is “Small AI”?

Small AI is a targeted and use-case-driven approach to artificial intelligence development.

Unlike general-purpose AI systems that require extensive computing and data-centre infrastructure, Small AI focuses on using specific capabilities to solve a clearly defined problem.

A Small AI solution may operate through accessible technologies such as:

Basic mobile phones

Sensors

Microcontrollers

Locally operated models

SMS-based interfaces

Voice-based systems

Devices with limited processing capacity

Systems that function with intermittent or restricted connectivity

A solution may use predictive, generative or agentic AI. The decisive issue is not the size or complexity of the model but whether the technology addresses a real problem within the operating environment of its intended users.

Effective Small AI solutions should be designed around:

A specific development problem

Clearly identified users

Local data and knowledge

Limited or unreliable connectivity

Affordable and accessible devices

Familiar communication channels

Measurable development outcomes

Responsible and inclusive implementation

Realistic infrastructure and institutional conditions

The World Bank also stresses that Small AI still depends on enabling foundations such as broadband access, digital literacy and trusted local institutions. Without these foundations, even technically promising solutions may remain isolated pilots instead of becoming sustainable and scalable interventions.

Challenge Areas

Every applicant must select one of the three official sector challenges.

Health

Applicants selecting health must develop an AI solution that responds to the relevant development challenge and operating conditions identified in the official sector brief.

Solutions will need to demonstrate how Small AI can contribute practical value in contexts where communities may face limitations in connectivity, devices, infrastructure, information or access to services.

Agriculture

Agriculture applicants must consider how targeted AI applications can create measurable value for agricultural stakeholders in resource-constrained environments.

The proposed technology should be grounded in a specific problem and should account for the digital tools, data, infrastructure and institutional conditions that must be present for the solution to work.

Tourism

Applicants selecting tourism must develop a practical solution that responds to the official tourism-sector challenge.

The proposal should show how AI can produce meaningful benefits within the sector while remaining accessible, context-specific and realistic about connectivity and technology constraints.

Applicants should consult the official sector briefs and avoid attempting to address all three sectors in one entry. The World Bank’s rules require each entry to respond to one sectoral challenge.

What Participants Must Build

The hackathon requires participants to build a working Small AI solution during the official competition weekend.

The proposed solution should:

Address one clearly defined challenge in health, agriculture or tourism.

Operate within the realities of a constrained environment.

Demonstrate a clear advantage over existing approaches.

Produce measurable or credible development value.

Consider accessibility and inclusion.

Reflect local needs, users and operating conditions.

Explain the infrastructure and preconditions required for implementation.

Acknowledge relevant technical, social and development trade-offs.

Comply with the technical and submission rules published by Hack-Nation.

Be submitted through the official competition platform during the prescribed window.

The broader Hack-Nation programme describes the event as a 24-hour global building experience delivered online and through physical hubs. Participants are expected to move from identifying a problem to developing and presenting a working AI product.
