TITLE: Science Granting Councils Initiative’s PPP Project Promotes Cooperation for Shared Access to Research Facilities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Access to and sharing of scientific research facilities, such as laboratories, experimental farms, and space launch installations, are essential for modern scientific inquiry. In the 21st century, the specialized and sophisticated research infrastructure required for cutting-edge research is often prohibitively expensive, making it difficult for individual institutions to acquire and maintain on their own. In addition, research and academic institutions tend to acquire these advanced research facilities and equipment at different times. Furthermore, most research and academic institutions in sub-Saharan Africa lack their own searchable databases of research facilities and equipment, and the up-to-date status of the available facilities across institutions is unknown. This has led to disparities in the availability and accessibility of research facilities within and across institutions.

These persistent disparities necessitate the development of research facilities and equipment-sharing guiding frameworks, policies, protocols, and a digital searchable platform for research and academic institutions. By promoting the sharing of research facilities and equipment, we can address these challenges through cost-sharing, improving resource utilization, and reducing the need for researchers to seek resources outside their countries and the African continent. This approach also fosters collaboration and knowledge exchange among researchers and institutions. Additionally, access to well-maintained, professionally operated facilities saves researchers time and money by eliminating the need for extensive equipment training.Sharing research facilities significantly impacts intellectual property (IP) development. Innovations and inventions rely on scientific skills and access to advanced research facilities and equipment. By sharing research facilities and equipment, we avoid resource duplication, ensuring funds are used effectively to acquire a diverse range of necessary infrastructure. This cost-effective approach supports national research and development (R&D) by providing comprehensive access to state-of-the-art facilities. This also aligns well with the principles of inclusivity and open science.

Despite these benefits, research facility sharing in Sub-Saharan Africa is limited due to various factors, including nonexistent or suboptimal frameworks such as institutional policies and signed Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs), conflicting stakeholder expectations, regulatory hurdles, intellectual property concerns, and financial considerations. Furthermore, the need for efficient resource allocation and scheduling is essential to avoid conflicts and ensure fair access to facilities. Financial considerations also play a significant role, as clear agreements on cost-sharing, maintenance, and operational expenses are necessary to prevent disputes and maintain long-term sustainability.

In the context of the Science Granting Councils, it is critical to ensure that there are effective frameworks to guide the sharing of research facilities and equipment within and between institutions and guidelines for drafting MoUs and various policies promoting infrastructure sharing.

Objective 5 under theme 6 of the current phase of the SGCI project aims to support councils in customizing and implementing an infrastructure sharing protocol. This builds upon the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST)’s earlier work of developing ‘Technomart’, an online platform designed to facilitate research infrastructure sharing, collaboration, and enhanced peer-to-peer learning. To ensure the Technomart’s effectiveness, an enabling environment and institutional level governance structures are necessary to promote the sharing of research infrastructures through the platform.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) in collaboration with the UNCST, is implementig objective 5 of the SGCI PPP project in a bid to strengthen research infrastructure management using the Technomart. As a centralized digital repository of research and development (R&D) equipment and facilities, Technomart aims to improve discoverability and accessibility of research equipment and facilities, encourage and support the sharing of research resources within and between institutions across the SGCI participating countries, and foster collaboration through building a network for knowledge exchange and partnership among others.

Capacity building of Council Team Members

In August 2024, the Association of African Universities, in collaboration with the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology and the Scinnovent Centre organised a workshop in Malawi that sought to promote the adoption and implementation of an infrastructure sharing protocol and the Technomart platform to encourage the efficient utilization of available research and innovation infrastructure. This workshop was hosted by the National Commission for Science and Technology (NCST), Malawi, at the Sunbird Lilongwe Hotel in Malawi as part of the Scinnovent Centre’s Methodology Training Workshop on Developing Institutional IP Policies and Strategies. About 30 participants (of mixed gender) from the SGCI-participating countries—Botswana, Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Senegal, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe—were in attendance.

Also in attendance were representatives of public and private research institutes, representatives of public and private universities, policymakers in government, and representatives of intellectual property offices, among others. The recent workshop on research facility sharing brought together key stakeholders to address challenges and develop strategies for cooperation. Drawing inspiration from the Model Cooperation Protocol, participants discussed best practices and shared experiences to improve collaboration among researchers, institutions, funders, and Science Granting Councils.

The workshop yielded significant outcomes, including discussing actionable strategies and recommendations for enhancing cooperation and minimizing conflicts in research facility sharing. Participants also gained increased awareness of the infrastructure sharing protocol and the Technomart platform, which is expected to promote a culture of collaboration and shared responsibility in utilizing research facilities. Furthermore, the workshop identified common challenges and best practices in developing and implementing MOUs for research facility sharing, providing valuable insights for future collaborations. It marked a significant step towards fostering cooperation and optimizing research infrastructure utilization, facilitated by strong and effective Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) among involved partners.

TITLE: International Physics Competition 2026: Join the Global Online Physics Challenge for Cash Prizes and Certificates

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Submissions are open for the International Physics Competition 2026, also known as IPhyC 2026. Officially described as the “Education Program & Talent Search in Physics,” IPhyC is an international online initiative that allows participants to test their physics knowledge, strengthen their scientific reasoning and engage with problems extending beyond the conventional classroom curriculum.

The competition is conducted online, meaning participants can enter without travelling to another country or attending an in-person international event. It combines accessible introductory problems with advanced calculations, research-based questions and fast-paced assessments across three progressive rounds.

The Qualification Round is free to enter. Participants must download the official problem sheet, solve the questions and submit their work online by Sunday, 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0. Successful participants can progress to the Semi-Final and Final rounds, where they may compete for cash prizes, international honours, national awards and verifiable certificates.

What Is the International Physics Competition?

The International Physics Competition is an independent educational programme designed to make international physics challenges accessible through digital technology. It is coordinated by Edu.Harbour and brings together participants, teachers, schools and local representatives from different parts of the world.

Its purpose goes beyond ranking competitors. IPhyC aims to encourage curiosity about physics, introduce participants to unconventional problem formats and help them develop skills that can support future studies in science, technology, engineering and research.

According to the organizers, the programme is intended to supplement established national and international physics Olympiads rather than replace them. Its focus is broader accessibility, educational development and exposure to scientific research. Read more about IPhyC’s mission and structure.

Recognition is not limited to the nine cash-prize winners.

The awards structure includes:

Official participation certificates for valid participants;

Semi-Finalist certificates;

Bronze, Silver or Gold honours for Finalists, depending on performance;

Special certificates for first-, second- and third-prize winners;

National Award certificates; and

A special honorary note for professionally typeset Qualification Round solutions.

The top three participants from a country may receive National Awards if they obtain at least 50% of the available Final Round points. The organizers may also publish a list of leading national performers.

Certificates include verification codes that allow schools, universities and other institutions to confirm their authenticity through the IPhyC website.

Information Required for Submission

Applicants should prepare the following information before opening the submission form:

Correct full name;

Date of birth;

Current country and city of study;

Active email address;

A password containing at least eight characters;

Official name of the school or university;

Grade or university year applicable on 1 November 2026;

Completed Qualification Round solution file;

Teacher or school email address, if available;

Preferred communication language; and

Local IPhyC representative’s name, if applicable.

The teacher’s email address and local representative selection are optional.

Participants must enter their names and dates of birth accurately because these details are used on certificates. The organizers may verify the ages of prize winners.

How to Enter the International Physics Competition 2026

Follow these steps:

Visit the official IPhyC website.

Download the 2026 Qualification Round problem sheet.

Review all five problems carefully.

Solve as many problems as possible and show the reasoning behind each answer.

Type the solutions or prepare clear scans of handwritten work.

Combine everything into one accepted file.

Ensure that the file is smaller than 10 MB.

Open the official submission form.

Enter the required personal and academic details accurately.

Upload the solution file.

Read and accept the competition rules and data policy.

Submit before 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0.

Monitor the registered email address and participant account for confirmation and results.

Submissions are not accepted by email.

Collaboration, Academic Integrity and Cheating Rules

Every participant must submit an individual solution.

During the Qualification Round, participants may:

Work with classmates or friends to explore possible approaches;

Receive basic guidance from a teacher;

Consult books and online material for general definitions and scientific background; and

Discuss the underlying concepts.

They may not:

Copy another person’s exact solution;

Copy a completed solution from the internet;

Ask users on an online platform to solve the problems for them; or

Submit work that is not their own.

During the Semi-Final examination, participants cannot use external websites, books, notes or assistance from another person. A calculator is permitted in the Semi-Final Round, but artificial intelligence and translation tools are limited to understanding the research paper during the preparation period.

During the Final Round, calculators, external sources and assistance from others are prohibited. Only blank paper and a pencil may be used for notes.

Cheating, plagiarism, impersonation or the submission of falsified information can result in immediate disqualification and loss of any registration fee. Participants should read the complete IPhyC cheating policy before entering.

How to Prepare for IPhyC 2026

A strong preparation strategy should include the following:

1. Understand the three-round structure

The Qualification Round rewards complete reasoning and clear written solutions. The Semi-Final adds a supervised, time-limited research component, while the Final requires faster responses across different physics fields.

2. Review fundamental physics

Focus on essential principles in mechanics, electricity and magnetism, thermodynamics, optics, modern physics, fluids and related topics.

3. Practise presenting complete solutions

Do not provide only a numerical answer. Define the variables, identify the relevant physical law, show the calculations and state the final result clearly with the correct units.

4. Strengthen scientific reading skills

Practise reading research abstracts, identifying a paper’s main finding and connecting unfamiliar terminology to familiar physics principles.

5. Solve problems under time limits

Timed practice is particularly important for the supervised Semi-Final and fast-paced Final Round.

6. Learn from errors

After attempting a problem, compare the approach with an official or trusted solution. Identify whether the mistake came from conceptual understanding, algebra, units, interpretation or time management.

7. Use official preparation materials

Consult previous IPhyC problems, recommended textbooks and the resources available through the official training page.

Role of Teachers and Schools

Teachers are not required for the initial Qualification Round, but they can play a valuable role in sharing the competition, guiding students and supervising later stages.

Registered teachers may be able to:

View their students’ results and certificates;

Download teacher reports;

Pay Semi-Final fees for multiple students as a group;

Supervise Semi-Final examinations; and

Access educational materials.

IPhyC also offers honorary awards for teachers and schools with significant participation, strong student performance or notable contributions. These awards do not include cash payments.

Language and Global Accessibility

English is the original language of IPhyC. The website also provides translated interfaces in German, Arabic, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian, Russian, Portuguese, Vietnamese, Japanese, Korean and Turkish.

The organizers indicate that non-English versions may contain automatic translations. Participants using a translated version should therefore compare any uncertain scientific wording with the original English material.

Because the competition is mainly online, no international travel is required. Participants should nevertheless ensure that they have reliable internet access and the necessary devices before any supervised examination.

Important Points to Remember

The Qualification Round is free, but the Semi-Final costs EUR 12.

Limited financial aid is available for eligible Semi-Finalists.

The Qualification Round deadline is 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0.

One solution file must be uploaded in an accepted format.

The file must be under 10 MB.

The same problems are given to all age groups.

Older groups have higher qualifying thresholds.

Personal information must be entered accurately for certificates.

All entries are individual, even where limited Qualification Round discussion is allowed.

Applicants should rely on the official website for any timetable changes.

Conclusion

The International Physics Competition 2026 offers an accessible way to test physics knowledge in an international setting without the cost and logistical burden of travelling overseas. Its three-round structure combines open-ended problem-solving, engagement with scientific research and supervised online assessments.

Participants can earn internationally verifiable certificates, compete for cash prizes and national recognition, and develop practical skills in scientific reasoning, analytical thinking and research comprehension. Anyone planning to enter should download the Qualification Round problem sheet immediately, prepare a complete and clearly presented solution, and submit well before the official deadline of 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0.

TITLE: AAU President, Prof. Kenneth Matengu and AAU Ambassador Prof. Nana Aba Appiah Amfo, Attain Key Global Leadership Roles on ACU Council

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) celebrates a proud and historic moment for African higher education. Two of our most distinguished leaders have ascended to high office within the Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU), placing the continent’s voice at the very heart of one of the world’s oldest and most influential university networks. This dual achievement highlights the global recognition of the leadership cultivated within the AAU’s membership and underscores our collective commitment to shaping the future of higher education worldwide.

Professor Kenneth Matengu, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Namibia and the elected President of the AAU Governing Board, was elected to the ACU Council in July 2025. He currently serves as a Council Member and Trustee, representing Constituency III – comprising East, West and Southern Africa – for a three-year term from 01 August 2025 to 31 July 2028. In a related recent and prestigious development, Professor Nana Aba Appiah Amfo, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ghana and the AAU Ambassador for Gender Equity & Social Inclusion, has been elected as the Chair of the ACU Council. She will provide strategic leadership for an initial two-year term, effective 1 January 2026, after having served as a valuable member of the Council since August 2024.

A Powerful Convergence of Governance and Advocacy

These appointments are not just personal accolades; they represent a strategic alignment of the AAU’s core missions on a global platform. Prof. Kenneth Matengu brings to the ACU Council his dynamic vision as the youngest-ever AAU President and his deep commitment to pan-African collaboration. His leadership is instrumental in driving initiatives that strengthen universities across the continent. Upon his election, Prof. Matengu stated his focus would be on “supporting postgraduate education and research, especially as Africa works to produce the next generation of doctoral graduates needed to realise our continent’s vision for the future.”

Prof. Nana Aba Appiah Amfo ascends to the ACU Chairmanship as a proven leader and a powerful voice for the values the AAU champions. Her role as our Ambassador for Gender Equity & Social Inclusion is a testament to her lifelong commitment to these principles. In her new role, she aims to “strengthen collaboration, advance equity and inclusion and ensure that higher education continues to serve as a powerful force for sustainable development and societal transformation.”

A Statement from the AAU Secretariat

The AAU community is immensely proud of Professors Matengu and Amfo. Their elections are a resounding endorsement of African leadership and the relevance of our continental agenda. To have our Board President on the ACU Council and our Ambassador for Gender Equity assuming its Chairmanship creates a unique and powerful synergy. It ensures that Africa’s priorities, from building research capacity to championing inclusive education, will be advocated for at the highest level of Commonwealth dialogue. This is a victory for every AAU member institution.

Celebrating Our Members, Elevating Our Continent

As the apex organisation for higher education in Africa, the AAU exists to connect, support, and celebrate the achievements of its members. The global recognition of Prof. Matengu and Prof. Amfo is a direct reflection of the excellence nurtured within the University of Namibia and the University of Ghana. We extend our heartfelt congratulations to these esteemed institutions for fostering such exemplary leadership.

We look forward to the strengthened partnership between the AAU and the ACU under this joint leadership. Their roles promise to foster greater collaboration, drive innovative solutions to shared challenges, and ensure that African universities continue to play a pivotal role in the global knowledge ecosystem.

TITLE: Artists’ Contacts 2026: Apply for ifa International Arts and Cultural Exchange Funding for Projects in 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen (ifa) Artists’ Contacts programme 2026 is offering funding for international artistic and cultural exchange projects connecting Germany with countries of the Global South and countries in transition. The programme is designed to strengthen international collaboration, encourage knowledge exchange, support artistic mobility and create sustainable networks among artists and cultural practitioners across borders.

Eligible applicants can seek support for a wide range of international visual arts and cultural activities, including working visits, research trips, exhibitions, artist-in-residence programmes, workshops, lectures, conferences, performances and other international exchange initiatives.

The application deadline is 30 September 2026, while supported projects are scheduled to take place between March and November 2027. Applicants who are interested in using art and cultural exchange to promote diversity, democratic values, human dignity, social cohesion and environmental responsibility are particularly encouraged to consider the programme.

About the ifa Artists’ Contacts Programme

The Artists’ Contacts programme is an international funding initiative of the Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen (ifa) that supports artistic and cultural exchange between Germany and countries in the Global South and countries in transition.

Rather than treating international mobility simply as an opportunity to travel, the programme places emphasis on meaningful cooperation, mutual learning and the creation of long-term relationships between cultural practitioners and institutions.

The programme is particularly relevant to artists and cultural professionals who want to work across national and cultural boundaries, develop collaborative artistic projects, undertake research, participate in international exhibitions or residencies, and build sustainable professional networks.

According to ifa, international artistic encounters can create spaces for dialogue, encourage different perspectives and contribute to mutual understanding. The programme therefore recognises art and culture as important tools for strengthening democratic values, social participation and responsible engagement with global challenges.

What Is the Main Focus of Artists’ Contacts 2026?

The central focus of the programme is intercultural exchange and networking in the visual arts.

The funding supports projects that place collaboration and knowledge exchange at the heart of international artistic engagement. Applicants are therefore encouraged to develop projects that go beyond one-time travel or isolated activities and instead demonstrate the potential to establish lasting relationships and professional networks.

The programme is especially interested in projects that contribute to:

International artistic and cultural cooperation

Knowledge exchange between cultural practitioners

Sustainable international networks

Diversity and inclusion

Democratic values

Human dignity

Social cohesion

Social participation

Environmental sustainability

Regional connections

Long-term international partnerships

Projects should demonstrate strong artistic quality while also reflecting the broader values promoted by ifa.

Who Can Benefit From the Artists’ Contacts Funding?

The programme is open to a broad range of professionals and organisations working in the arts and cultural sector.

Potential beneficiaries include:

Artists

Curators

Art mediators and art educators

Art theorists

Architects

Designers

Photographers

Media artists

Institutions working within the arts and cultural sector

The programme is therefore not limited to one particular artistic discipline. Instead, it provides opportunities for a variety of visual arts and cultural practitioners to participate in international exchange and collaborative projects.

Applicants should, however, ensure that their proposed project meets the programme’s artistic, collaborative and international eligibility requirements.

Which Countries Are Eligible?

A major feature of the Artists’ Contacts programme is its focus on international cooperation between Germany and countries included on the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) list of developing and transition countries.

Applications can be submitted from countries on the DAC list for projects taking place in Germany. Applications from Germany can also be submitted for projects taking place in eligible countries on the DAC list.

This means that the programme provides a two-way framework for cultural exchange:

Artists and cultural practitioners from eligible DAC countries can participate in projects in Germany.

Artists and cultural practitioners based in Germany can undertake eligible projects in countries appearing on the DAC list.

Applicants should consult the current official list of eligible countries before preparing their applications because eligibility depends on the country’s inclusion on the relevant DAC list.

Importantly, eligibility is not determined by race or ethnicity. The programme’s geographic eligibility is based on the relevant DAC country classification and the applicant’s location or residence in accordance with the programme rules.

Key Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should carefully review the programme requirements before submitting a proposal. The following conditions are particularly important.

1. The Project Must Demonstrate High Artistic Quality

The planned project should have a strong artistic or cultural concept and demonstrate a high level of artistic quality.

Applicants should clearly communicate what they intend to achieve, why the project is artistically significant and how the proposed international collaboration contributes to the development of the work or professional practice.

2. Projects Should Reflect ifa’s Values

In addition to artistic quality, ifa considers broader values when assessing applications.

These include:

Social relevance

Diversity

Environmental sustainability

Regional connections

International cooperation

Social cohesion

Democratic values

Applicants should therefore avoid presenting international travel as an end in itself. A stronger application should explain the artistic, cultural and social value of the proposed exchange.

3. International Artistic Cooperation Is Required

The project must involve artistic and content-based cooperation between Germany and eligible countries in transition or countries of the Global South listed under the DAC framework.

The international dimension of the project is therefore fundamental to the programme.

4. Special Residence Requirements Apply to Projects in Germany

For projects involving travel to Germany, the participating artistic and cultural workers from eligible developing or transition countries must come from a country on the DAC list and must currently live there.

This requirement is important for applicants who may have nationality from an eligible country but currently reside elsewhere.

5. Additional Residence Requirement for Projects Outside Germany

For projects taking place in an eligible DAC country, artistic and cultural workers who do not have German citizenship must have lived in Germany for at least five years.

The programme does not fund trips to the applicant’s country of origin under this arrangement.

6. An Institutional Invitation Is Generally Required

Applicants normally need an invitation from a non-commercial cultural or exhibition organisation or an artist-in-residence establishment.

The organisation should not be a profit-oriented gallery.

An invitation is not required for research trips.

The foreign institution issuing the invitation must also provide significant financial and/or other services as part of the project.

7. Commercial Projects Are Not Eligible

The project must not be organised within a commercial context.

For example, projects connected to commercial art fairs are not eligible. The sale of artworks also excludes a project from funding.

This means applicants should clearly distinguish an artistic or cultural exchange project from a commercial activity.

8. Students Cannot Apply

Projects by students are not eligible for Artists’ Contacts funding.

ifa recommends that students seeking relevant international academic opportunities instead explore programmes offered by the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD).

What Activities Can the Funding Support?

Artists’ Contacts funding can support a wide range of artistic and cultural exchange activities.

Eligible activities can include:

Exhibitions

Performances

Artist-in-residence programmes

Workshops

Preparatory trips

Research trips

Working visits

International symposia

Conferences

Lectures

Other international exchange initiatives

This broad range of activities makes the programme relevant to artists and cultural professionals at different stages of an international project.

A research-oriented applicant, for example, may use the opportunity to undertake an international research trip, while another applicant may use the programme to participate in an exhibition, workshop, residency or international cultural event.

What Costs Does the Programme Cover?

The Artists’ Contacts programme provides support for travel and accommodation costs in accordance with the applicable Federal Travel Expenses Act.

For artistic and cultural workers travelling from countries in transition and developing countries to participate in eligible projects, ifa can cover a number of expenses.

These may include:

Flight expenses

Travel expenses

Accommodation costs

Visa costs

Overseas health insurance

Daily food allowance of EUR 28 per day

The programme does not cover travel and care expenses for family members.

For Germans and artistic and cultural workers who have lived in Germany for at least five years and are travelling to eligible countries outside Germany, support can include the following:

Flight expenses

Travel expenses

Accommodation costs

Visa costs

Applicable daily food allowances

Again, family members’ travel and care costs cannot be covered by the programme.

Environmental Sustainability Is an Important Consideration

The programme recognises that international cultural exchange often requires travel, which can have an environmental impact.

For this reason, ifa encourages applicants to consider environmental sustainability from the earliest stages of project planning.

Applicants are encouraged to:

Consider the environmental impact of international travel.

Prioritise sustainable forms of mobility where practical.

Reduce the carbon footprint of their projects.

Incorporate environmental considerations into project planning.

Demonstrate responsible use of environmental resources.

Environmental sustainability is also one of the aspects considered when assessing the overall quality and relevance of proposed projects.

How to Apply for the Artists’ Contacts Programme

The application process involves four main steps.

Step 1: Request Access to the Online Application

Applicants must first request access through the official Artists’ Contacts application system.

Step 2: Open the Link Sent by Email

After requesting access, applicants receive an email containing a link through which they can create their online application.

Step 3: Complete the Application

Applicants should complete all required sections of the application.

The system allows applicants to save their work and return to it later, meaning the application does not necessarily have to be completed in a single session.

Step 4: Submit the Online Application and Send the Signed Hard Copy

After submitting the online application, applicants must print it, sign it and send the hard copy by post to:

ifa – Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen

Artists’ Contacts

Charlottenplatz 17

D-70173 Stuttgart

Germany

Applicants should allow sufficient time for the physical application to reach the organisation because the postmark deadline applies.

APPLY HERE

Documents Required for the Application

Applicants should prepare the required supporting documents before submitting their application.

The official programme lists the following key documents:

Invitation Letter

Applicants generally need an invitation from the relevant foreign cultural or exhibition organisation, unless the application concerns a research trip.

Description of the Host Institution

Applicants should provide information describing the cultural or exhibition institution involved in the project.

Curriculum Vitae

CVs should be submitted for all applicants for whom funding is being requested.

The CVs should help demonstrate the applicants’ artistic or professional backgrounds and their suitability for the proposed project.

Visual Material

Applicants should provide visual material relating to the proposed project and/or examples of previous artistic work.

This is particularly important because the programme evaluates the artistic quality of applications.

Airfare Quotations

Applicants must provide three quotations for airfare based on current fares.

Applicants should therefore obtain current and credible flight quotations when preparing the budget and supporting documentation.

Sound and video works can be provided as links in the upload section of the application system.

Application Deadline for Artists’ Contacts 2026

The official application deadline is 30 September 2026.

The funding is for projects taking place between March and November 2027.

Applicants should pay close attention to the deadline because ifa states that no additional applications for projects taking place in 2027 will be accepted after 30 September 2026.

The date of the postmark applies, and applications sent after the deadline will not be considered.

Important Deadline Information

Application deadline: 30 September 2026

Eligible project period: March to November 2027

Notification of decision: February 2027

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day because the process involves both an online submission and a signed hard-copy application sent by post.

Visit HERE for more information about the Artists’ Contacts Programme 2026.

What Happens After You Apply?

Once applications have been submitted, they are assessed through the programme’s annual selection process.

An expert jury meets once a year to decide which projects will receive funding.

Funding decisions and the amount awarded depend on the available IFA budget and the applications received.

Applicants will receive written notification of acceptance or rejection in February 2027.

Applicants should also be aware of several important conditions surrounding the decision-making process:

No reasons for funding or rejection decisions will be provided.

Rejected applications cannot be resubmitted.

There is no legal recourse against the decision.

Additional materials submitted with an application will not be returned.

Projects that begin before approval cannot receive retrospective funding.

Expenses incurred before approval cannot be reimbursed retrospectively.

These conditions make it particularly important for applicants to wait for formal approval before beginning activities for which they expect to receive funding.

How Can Applicants Strengthen Their Proposals?

Although funding decisions are made by an expert jury and no outcome can be guaranteed, applicants can improve the clarity and competitiveness of their proposals by presenting a well-developed project.

A strong proposal should clearly explain:

What the project is about – Describe the artistic or cultural concept in clear terms.

Why international cooperation is necessary – Explain why collaboration across Germany and the partner country adds value.

Who is involved—Introduce the artists, cultural practitioners and host institutions.

What the project will achieve – Define the expected artistic and cultural outcomes.

How knowledge will be exchanged – Explain how participants will learn from one another.

How the project can create lasting relationships—Demonstrate potential for continued cooperation after the funded activity.

How the project reflects IFA’s values—Address diversity, social relevance, environmental sustainability and regional connections where appropriate.

How the budget will be used – Ensure requested travel-related costs are clearly justified.

Why the proposed activities are appropriate – Link each activity to the project’s objectives.

How environmental impacts will be considered – Explain efforts to make international mobility as sustainable as reasonably possible.

Applicants should also ensure that all required supporting documents are complete and consistent with the project proposal.

Why Artists and Cultural Practitioners Should Consider This Opportunity

International collaboration can be expensive, particularly when it involves air travel, accommodation, visas and other international mobility costs.

The Artists’ Contacts programme can reduce some of these financial barriers and make international artistic cooperation more accessible.

The opportunity can be particularly valuable for professionals seeking to:

Expand their international networks.

Collaborate with artists and cultural organisations across borders.

Develop new artistic projects.

Participate in exhibitions or performances.

Undertake international research.

Join artist-in-residence programmes.

Organise workshops and knowledge-sharing activities.

Participate in international conferences, symposia and lectures.

Establish long-term institutional partnerships.

Explore new cultural perspectives.

Connect artistic practice with social and environmental issues.

Beyond the immediate financial assistance, the programme’s emphasis on sustainable international networks means that applicants can frame their projects around longer-term professional and cultural relationships rather than short-term travel alone.

Important Restrictions Applicants Should Know

Before applying, prospective applicants should carefully consider the programme’s restrictions.

The following are particularly important:

Commercial projects are not eligible.

Art fairs and similar commercial activities do not qualify.

Selling artworks excludes funding.

Student projects are not eligible.

Trips to an applicant’s country of origin are not permitted in the relevant projects involving non-German citizens residing in Germany.

Projects that have already started cannot receive retrospective funding.

Expenses incurred before approval cannot be reimbursed retrospectively.

Family members’ travel and care expenses are not covered.

Applicants cannot resubmit rejected applications.

Funding is subject to the available budget.

Approved funding represents the maximum amount payable subject to the relevant rules and receipts.

The ifa Artists’ Contacts 2026 funding programme presents an important opportunity for artists, curators, art mediators, art theorists, architects, designers and cultural institutions seeking to develop meaningful international collaborations between Germany and eligible countries in the Global South and countries in transition.

Through support for travel, accommodation, visas, insurance and daily allowances, the programme can help reduce some of the financial barriers associated with international artistic mobility. TITLE: Who Teaches the Teachers and Who Will?

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
By Daniel Omanyo and Izel Kipruto

Kenya’s education reforms are ambitious, but their success hinges on a question too often overlooked: Who Teaches the Teachers and Who Will? Behind every well-trained teacher stands a university lecturer shaping the quality of learning for millions. Yet evidence shows our higher education system is straining under growing demand and shrinking faculty capacity. Kenya faces a critical shortage of university faculty to prepare teachers for the Competency-Based Education (CBE). Investing in those who teach the teachers is important for lasting reform.

What the data show

Recent findings from the Demographics of African Faculty in the East African Community (DAF-EAC) project, a collaboration between Education Sub Saharan Africa (ESSA), the Inter-University Council for East Africa, the Association of African Universities, and the Population Reference Bureau, paint a clear picture of this challenge.

Across East Africa, student enrolment in universities has surged over the past decade, but faculty recruitment has not kept pace. In Kenya, for instance, the DAF-EAC study shows that no discipline currently meets the student–teacher ratio targets set out in the 2014 Universities Regulations. The situation is most pressing in Faculties of Education, where the Commission for University Education recommends a ratio of 15 students per lecturer. In reality, the average ratio stands at 53 to 1.

Put simply, one lecturer may be responsible for teaching and mentoring more than fifty students, over three times the recommended number. This makes it difficult to give students the personalised attention they need, engage in quality research, or develop innovative teaching methods. Yet, this data also highlights an opportunity: investing in and strengthening faculty capacity can directly improve the quality of university education, research, and innovation across Kenya and the region.

Why it matters

Teacher educators sit at the heart of Kenya’s education system. They are the ones who prepare teachers to bring our education reforms to life, from early childhood to tertiary and technical training. Their ability to provide quality instruction, mentorship, and research guidance directly shapes the quality of learning in classrooms across the country. At the recent Education Evidence for Action conference held at Embu University, under the theme “Reimagining Teacher Education for Sustainable Development in Africa,” this issue took centre stage. In his keynote remarks, the Cabinet Secretary for Education referenced the DAF-EAC findings, noting that Kenya may need to recruit about 35,000 new faculty members by 2030 to meet university staffing norms. This acknowledgement is a positive sign that policy decisions are increasingly being guided by evidence. Strengthening the higher education workforce is not just about numbers, it is about ensuring that the next generation of teachers, and in turn learners, receive the quality education they deserve. Building a stronger faculty base today will make Kenya’s education system more resilient, responsive, and ready for the future. The urgency of this issue is clear. The recent lecturers’ strike laid bare long-standing concerns about pay, workload, and morale across universities. It echoes the DAF-EAC findings and reminds us that lasting education reform depends not only on policy and staffing targets, but also on valuing and supporting those who teach the teachers.

Learning from broader trends

Kenya’s experience reflects a wider continental pattern. A recent study by the Research on Socio-Economic Policy at Stellenbosch University found that half of South African teachers are considering leaving the profession within the next decade, largely due to burnout and heavy workloads. While the contexts differ, the lesson is universal: when educators, whether in schools or universities, feel overstretched and undervalued, the quality of education inevitably suffers. Preventing similar pressures within higher education must therefore be a national priority.

Pathways forward

Addressing the faculty shortage requires more than filling vacancies. It demands a comprehensive, long-term strategy that balances recruitment with sustained investment in professional growth and institutional support. Kenya can take several key actions to strengthen its higher education workforce. This includes building robust data systems to guide evidence-based planning and forecasting, improving working conditions and incentives to make academic careers more attractive to young professionals, and expanding professional development opportunities in pedagogy, research, and technology. Equally important is promoting mentorship and succession planning to nurture the next generation of scholars and leaders within universities. As Kenya embraces digital learning and the opportunities of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, teacher educators must be equipped to integrate emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, into their teaching. By doing so, they can help ensure that Africa’s young people are not only consumers of technology but also creators of innovation.

Building a sustainable future

Budget limits are real, but DAF-EAC data show that targeted, evidence-led planning can direct scarce resources where they matter most. The cost of inaction is far higher: overcrowded classes, falling quality, and an education system struggling to meet its promise. Kenya has expanded access and reformed its curriculum. The next step is clear, invest in the people who make that system work: those who teach the teachers. By prioritising faculty recruitment, development, and wellbeing, Kenya can rebuild the foundation of its education system and ensure every learner is guided by a motivated, well-prepared, and innovative teacher. Because the real question isn’t whether we can afford to invest in teacher educators, but whether we can afford not to.

Daniel Omanyo is the Research Manager, and Izel Kipruto is the Head of Communications at ESSA

TITLE: CERHI/ACEGID Partnership Wins Grant for Validation of Rapid Diagnostic COVID-19 Test Kits

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Centre of Excellence in Reproductive Health Innovation (CERHI), University of Benin in collaboration with the African Centre of Excellence in Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID) hosted by the Redeemer’s University and the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH) have been awarded a Grant to validate Rapid Diagnostic Tests kits (RDT) for COVID-19 testing in Nigeria.

The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a research consortium between CERHI and UBTH for the testing of the SARS COV-2 virus. With CERHI’s laboratories and facilities, including RT-PCR machine for testing for the virus and UBTH’s expertise in managing infectious diseases, the unit was validated by the Nigerian Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) to become the second testing unit in Edo State, and one of the few in Nigeria. Similarly, the African Centre of Excellence in Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID) successfully sequenced the genomes of the COVID-19 virus and was the first institution to do so in Africa. Considering this knowledge and expertise, the three institutions partnered to apply for a Grant on the validation of RDTs in Nigeria. Led by Professor Friday E. Okonofua, Centre leader of CERHI and Professor Christian Happi, Centre Leader of ACEGID, the team’s proposal was selected for funding and implementation. The CERHI/UBTH/ACEGID team is one of the 5 teams selected to develop and implement a national protocol for the validation of RDT kits for COVID-19 in Nigeria. The projected timeline for completion of this project is four months.

The importance of this project stems from the fact that available rapid tests for COVID-19 in Nigeria have not been validated and as a result, this project will contribute to the validation of the rapid COVID-19 tests, comparing the sensitivities and predictive results obtained from their use with the gold standard and the PCR test. If the rapid tests are found to be sensitive and accurate, it will expand access to COVID-19 testing to millions of Nigerians, and the continent at large.

The Centre of Excellence in Reproductive Health Innovation (CERHI) and Centre of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID) are part of the 53 Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) supported by World Bank through the coordination of the Association of African Universities as the Regional Facilitation Unit. The ACE Impact project aims to address regional developmental challenges through quality post-graduate education and applied research (https://ace.aau.org/).

CERHI implements high quality training and applied research for reproductive health professionals. The centre is also a leading name in the development and implementation of several ground-breaking researches in the field of sexual and reproductive health and population studies within the continent (https://www.cerhiuniben.edu.ng/).

ACEGID focuses on capacity building of African scientists in the field of genomics. The centre aims to translate the research outcome to products that can be deployed to the field to contribute to the control, management and elimination of infectious diseases in the continent (https://acegid.org/).

TITLE: Building the Capacities of African Universities in Research and Project Proposal Grants Writing: AAU Takes the Lead

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) is leading the retooling and upskilling of staff from African Universities in Research and Project Grants writing through hosting a series of capacity building workshops.

The workshops, which started on February 17th -March 10th, 2021 attracted participants from Kenya, Zambia, Nigeria, Zimbabwe, Lesotho, Eswatini, Uganda, among other African countries.

Dr. Violet Makuku, the Quality Assurance Specialist, Workshops Coordinator and facilitator of the workshop, encouraged participants to be vigilant and always be on the lookout for opportunities as there are many grant calls which are frequently released that a lot of stakeholders in African HEIs, including the workshop participants, do not get to know of.

Even in cases where they were aware of such calls and respond to them, some knowledge and skills gaps have led to their inability to win those grants. This trend forms part of the background which informed the AAU to move to improve capacity in this area, with an ultimate target of helping more African Universities to actually win the grants when they submit their proposals in response to a specific call.

Taking participants through the sessions, Dr. Makuku highlighted that both Solicited and Unsolicited Proposals require high levels of dedication, knowledge, skills, time and hard work to win them. She explained that with Solicited Proposals, a taskforce need to devote quality time to search for them (via the internet and other sources). The need to also subscribe to some channels/websites so that stakeholders are notified immediately there is a call for proposals was shared by her.

She also stressed the following key issues to consider when writing proposals and these include but are not limited to, having a policy in place, building good track records, adopting multi-disciplinary and inter-disciplinary approaches, teamwork and collaboration, monitoring and evaluation as well as effective communication. Participants were encouraged to, “Build strong grant proposal writing teams which are so strong to an extent that no one will know who the leader of the team is.” She stated this when she spoke about teamwork and collaboration.

She explained that the Multidisciplinary and Interdisciplinary Approaches cover gaps and strengthen the case in a proposal. Citing an example of a research proposal on “Causes of increase in Malaria deaths in a given Community”, she explained that if the writing of a proposal only include a team from the medical field, it will not help much, because other people like religious leaders, communication personnel, Accountants, Demography Experts, Traditional Healers, Policy Makers, Environmentalists, Community Based Organizations (CBOs), Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) are key players, and therefore should be involved so that they work hand in hand to win the grant.

Several other examples were cited to drum home the message that multi and interdisciplinary approaches were strategic choices. One of such was the example of a proposal on, “The Cause of High Mortality Rate due to Malaria in a given Community.” She intimated that such a proposal would require among others, an environmentalist, to research on mosquito breeding places in that area and an editor to check and correct grammatical, typographical and other errors in the proposal.

Overall, she stressed on the need for hard work in the pursuit of grants and in the entire process of grant writing – “It is only through hard work and dedication that we can deliver a strong economy and create opportunities for all”, she remarked. Dr Makuku cited how in 2020, Prof. William Bazeyo, an academician in Uganda won a UGX 185 billion grant which benefited his country through the Makerere University and the Ministry of Health by determination and hard work, as an example. According to her, this was an unprecedented situation.

At the end of the session, Dr. Makuku highlighted the need to have sound knowledge and skills in academic writing and research methodology. She indicated that these are some of the workshops the AAU offers at international and institutional levels. She also urged institutions who are non- AAU members to register and become members to help take African Higher and Tertiary Education to the highest level. Participants and stakeholders in general, were also encouraged to visit the AAU website (www.aau.org) and blog (blog.aau.org) for further information on the Association, and its various initiatives.

By Pamela H. Boamah (Association of African Universities Workshops Unit)

TITLE: Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program, Spring 2022

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Application now open for the next competition of the
Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program (CADFP)
DEADLINE: February 28, 2022 at 11:59 PM EST

The Institute of International Education (IIE) is pleased to announce that the next round of competition for the CADFP is now open.
Apply now or share this message with those who might be interested.

What is the CADFP?
The CADFP is a scholar exchange program for African higher education institutions to host a diaspora scholar for 14-90 days for projects in curriculum co-development, research collaboration and graduate student teaching and mentoring.

Who is eligible?

Accredited universities in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania and Uganda, and member institutions of the African Research Universities Alliance (ARUA) (including Addis Ababa University, Ethiopia; the University of Rwanda; Cheikh Anta Diop University, Senegal; and University of Mauritius) can submit a project request to host a scholar.

Scholars born in Africa, who live in the United States or Canada and work in an accredited college or university in either of those two countries, can apply online to be placed on a roster of candidates for a fellowship. Scholars must hold a terminal degree in their field and may hold any academic rank.

How do I apply?
Links and information about the African host institution project request application, scholar roster application and review guidelines are posted on the CADFP website. Interested parties are invited to register for one of the informational webinars:

Information for Diaspora Scholars, Webinar #1: Thursday, January 13 at 11 AM Eastern US Time
Information for Potential Hosts: Wednesday, January 19 at 10 AM South Africa Standard Time
Information for Diaspora Scholars, Webinar #2: Thursday, January 27 at 12 noon Eastern US Time

After the webinars, the recordings will be posted via the YouTube Channel.

Timeline
The deadline for project requests from host universities and scholar applications for diaspora scholars is February 28, 2022 at 11:59 pm EST. Selection decisions will be made in March-April 2022; project visits can begin as early as June 1, 2022 and must be completed by November 30, 2023.

Benefits
Selected fellows receive a $150/day stipend, visa costs, limited health insurance, round-trip international air travel and ground transportation costs to and from home and the U.S./Canadian airport. Selected Host Fellows and Diaspora Fellows can apply for supplemental funds to be used for fieldwork, publication costs and workshops. The CADFP Team manages the fellowships and payments to fellows. Host institutions are encouraged to provide cost-share for the fellow’s meals, lodging and in-country transportation.

For more information on the fellowship program and application process, as well as the projects of current fellows, please write to AfricanDiaspora@iie.org visit their website and communities on Facebook and Twitter.

TITLE: Njala University and eLearnLXD Announce $250,000 Scholarship Fund for Civil Servants in Sierra Leone’s First Online MBA Program

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana – December 1st, 2025 – Njala University and eLearnLXD have unveiled a $250,000 partial scholarship program to support 500 civil servant professionals enrolling in Sierra Leone’s first fully online Master of Business Administration (MBA) program. Each accepted student will be eligible for up to $500 in financial assistance, dramatically reducing the cost barrier to advanced business education for public sector professionals across Africa.

This landmark initiative, developed through a strategic partnership between the Association of African Universities (AAU) and eLearnLXD/eLearnAfricaLMS, represents a significant advancement in making quality postgraduate education accessible to working professionals throughout Africa, especially the ECOWAS sub-region. The program is delivered through the innovative eLearnAfricaLXD platform, offering flexible self-paced learning with live interactive discussions and multimedia coursework accessible from any location.

The program aligns with President Julius Maada Bio’s vision for education as a cornerstone of national development. As stated in The Calabash Newspaper, President Bio emphasized, “We already know the impact of education as a cross-cutting driver for inclusive and sustainable development. Nations that have achieved rapid and sustainable economic growth have done so by developing the most productive resource in any nation: human capital.”

Vice-Chancellor Prof. Bashiru Koroma reinforced this commitment, “Collaborating with eLearnLXD enables us to deliver an MBA that is both accessible and aligned with the region’s economic and professional priorities. This initiative represents our dedication to building public sector capacity through targeted educational opportunities that support the nation’s human capital development agenda.”

“This initiative shows what’s possible when African institutions embrace technology for inclusion. We are particularly focused on creating pathways for civil servants who represent the backbone of public service delivery across the continent,” Brook Negussie, CEO of eLearnAfricaLMS, noted in highlighting the transformative potential of the partnership.

The program has already garnered positive feedback from current participants, with one student noting, “This is a different ball game. The quality is exceptional — the standard is on another level.”

Aligning with both ECOWAS Vision 2050 and the African Union’s Agenda 2063, the online MBA program emphasizes education and innovation as key drivers of sustainable development. The curriculum strategically integrates core business subjects with essential modern competencies in digital leadership, ethics, and applied research, preparing graduates for critical leadership roles, including Operations Manager, CFO, HR Director, IT Project Manager, and Policy Advisor.

Applications for the third cohort of the Njala University Online MBA are now being accepted from qualified civil servants and other professionals across Africa.

Apply now – https://airtable.com/appAmYM1s4O2iWjNY/pagjXFMSlAPXGZFvQ/form

Learn more here – https://njala-mba.netlify.app/

For further inquiries or assistance, please feel free to contact us at your convenience: isaack@elearnafrica.com / sualiho@njala.edu.sl / sophiea@elearnafricalms.com or bobsonkamara74@gmail.com

About Njala University

Established in 1964, Njala University stands as one of Sierra Leone’s premier higher education institutions, following the American Land Grant University model. With campuses spanning Moyamba, Bo, Bonthe, and Freetown, the university offers comprehensive programs across Education, Agricultural Sciences, Law, Social Sciences, and Information Technology.

About eLearnAfrica

eLearnAfrica is a mission-driven social enterprise dedicated to expanding educational access and professional development opportunities across Africa. Through its partnership with the Association of African Universities, the organization operates the AAU–eLearnAfricaLMS platform, launched in 2021 with an ambitious goal of reaching 10 million learners continent-wide.

TITLE: The University of London Awards Professor Bakri Osman Saeed the Degree of Honorary Professor

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Professor Bakri Osman Saeed, President of the Association of African Universities (AAU) Governing Board and President of Sudan International University, has been appointed an honorary Professor by Queen Mary College – University of London (QMUL). The AAU congratulates Prof. Saeed for his remarkable contributions and outstanding efforts in elevating the AAU’s presence on the global stage.

In the United Kingdom, this is the highest title bestowed by a British university on individuals whom the university wishes to appoint, honor and work with. Queen Mary College – University of London considers this appointment an important means that enables the university to establish relationships with people who are distinguishing themselves either in their own academic disciplines or in fields of activities where QMUL would benefit from association. Through this means, QMUL enriches the breadth of its community and the breadth of people making contributions to its endeavours, as the university benefits from their skills and experience in contributing to university activities such as teaching, scientific research and community participation, in addition to contributing to the design and development of the university’s strategy for internationalization and global engagement.

Profile of Prof. Bakri Osman Saeed – President of the AAU Governing Board

Prof. Bakri Osman Saeed obtained a Bachelors degree in Medicine and Surgery from the University of Khartoum, a PhD from the University of Leeds in the UK, a Doctor of Medicine from the University of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, a Fellowship of the Royal College of Pathologists, and a Fellowship of the Royal College of Physicians, London, UK. He is currently the President of the Association of African Universities (AAU) and the President of Sudan International University. He is a UNESCO Chair in School Health Education. Before that, he was the Founding Dean of St. George’s International Medical School, which is a partnership between St. George’s University in Grenada and Northumbria University in Newcastle-upon-Tyne. He started his career as a lecturer at the University of Khartoum, and then worked for many years as a Medical Consultant and Associate Professor at the University of Newcastle-upon-Tyne and the University of London (UCL).

He has been a Visiting Professor for University of Northumbria in Newcastle and St George’s University in Grenada, where he was a Consultant to the Caribbean Reference Laboratory. He has been involved with many higher education and training bodies in the UK and in many other countries. In Sudan, he contributed significantly to the development of higher education as a Chair or member of important bodies and committees, including: the committee for revising the Higher Education Act, the committee for the evaluation of research proposals, the Ministry of Higher Education, Sudan, and the committee for the regulation of private higher education. He was involved in conflict resolution and peace promotion in Africa through his appointment as Special Advisor to the United Nations University for Peace.

TITLE: Call for Applications: Takemi Fellowship at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Each year, the Takemi Program in International Health at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, recruits a small group of mid-career researchers and professionals to spend an academic year at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. The Takemi Program provides participants with the space, time, and flexibility to enhance their capacity for research and leadership. To do this, Fellows are linked to two key resources: the weekly Takemi Seminar Series, and expert faculty. In addition, Fellows have the opportunity for collaboration throughout the Harvard community, and may elect to deepen their knowledge of theory or practice through relevant coursework. Fellows draw on these resources to produce at least one paper of publishable quality.

Since 1984, 282 Fellows from 56 countries have trained in the Takemi Program.

Applications are due by December 31, 2018 at midnight EST.

This prestigious competition recognizes PhD students and recent doctoral graduates from around the world for their outstanding contributions to childhood disability research, enabling personalized versions of a good life across the lifespan for all individuals with childhood-onset disabilities, acquired injuries and developmental differences, their families and communities.

TITLE: Research Analyzes the Role of Ocean Heat Transport and Surface Heat Exchange in Warming the Arctic Ocean and Reducing Sea Ice

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
By Randy Showstack

With the Arctic Ocean warming much more rapidly than the global average over the past several decades, the extent and thickness of sea ice in the Arctic has decreased dramatically. Climate models project that these trends will accelerate even more in the future. A new analysis finds that increased ocean heat transport (OHT) into the Arctic through the Barents Sea Opening (BSO) is the primary driver of this warming, with OHT from the Fram and Bering straits also contributing to the warming. (See Figure 1 for a map of the region.)

Figure 1. Map indicating the location of the Arctic gateways where the ocean heat transport is calculated. (Illustration by Natalie Renier, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)

The analysis also finds that the projected future OHT changes are driven primarily by warmer inflowing water rather than by changes in the volume of water transported through those three Arctic gateways, according to the journal article, “The Respective Roles of Ocean Heat Transport and Surface Heat Fluxes in Driving Arctic Ocean Warming and Sea Ice Decline,” published in the American Meteorological Society’s Journal of Climate in January 2024.

In addition, the analysis calculates the contributions of ocean-ice and atmosphere-ice heat fluxes to the sea ice heat budget changes (see Figure 2), and determines that the ocean is likely to become the most important source of heat for the ice and hence the most responsible for the melting. “Throughout the entire twentieth century as well as the early twenty-first century, the atmosphere is the main contributor to ice heat gain in summer, though the ocean’s role is not negligible. However, over the course of the 21st century, the ocean progressively becomes the main heat source for the ice as the ocean warms,” according to the article.

Figure 2. Illustration of the factors that contribute to the ocean and sea-ice heat budgets. Credit: Natalie Renier from WHOI Graphics.

“The ocean is expected to play a very important role in driving sea-ice loss in the future. In particular, the increased heat inputs from the different Arctic Ocean gateways, particularly the Barents Sea Opening, the Fram Strait, and the Bering Strait from the Pacific side of the Arctic are going to be very important for driving active ocean warming,” said journal article lead author Dylan Oldenburg, a postdoctoral investigator in physical oceanography at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI). Co-authors are Young-Oh Kwon of WHOI; Claude Frankignoul with WHOI and Sorbonne University; and Gokhan Danabasoglu, Stephen Yeager, and Who M. Kim with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research.

For their heat budget analysis, the researchers defined the Arctic Ocean as the region bounded by the Arctic Ocean gateways, which include the Barents Sea Opening as well as the Barrow, Bering, Fram, and Nares straits. The analysis uses the 100-member Large Ensemble of the state-of-the-art fully coupled Community Earth System Model, version 2 (CESM2), focusing primarily on the period between 1920 and 2100. This Large Ensemble provides researchers with the ability to separate climate change signal variations from natural internal variability.

“The beauty of having so many ensemble members, or simulations, is that when you average them together, there is a lot less noise, and you can remove internal variability that shows up in each ensemble member,” said Oldenburg. “When you look at the Large Ensemble, you can isolate the response of the climate or the Arctic Ocean, for instance, to the greenhouse gas forcing without internal variability masking what is happening due to that forcing.”

Although the model has some minor drawbacks, such as underestimating the Fram Strait OHT relative to observations, overall CESM2 is a good model and the net volume transports through the Arctic gateways are well-represented relative to observations, the article noted. “For limited parts of the historical period, we can rely on observations. However, because observations in the Arctic Ocean are limited and we do not have observations of future conditions, we need to use models,” said Oldenburg. “Our results based on CESM2-LENS indicate an essential role for ocean heat transport in driving Arctic Ocean warming, in line with previous studies.”

The earlier studies have typically examined OHTs that are zonally integrated across a particular latitude, and not based on physical pathways into the Arctic Ocean, according to Oldenburg. The researchers here explicitly calculated the OHT across each of the Arctic gateways to determine the relative importance of OHTs across the gateways. All of the heat flux components are fairly constant in the ensemble mean until about 1980, when the total OHT into the Arctic starts to rapidly increase, eventually strengthening from 0.06 petawatts (PW) from 1961-1980 to 0.10 PW from 2081-2100. The total OHC change over the course of the simulations increases the mean Arctic Ocean temperature from 0.3° to 0.5° Celsius, according to the article. “The increase in the OHT into the Arctic in response to the external forcing results in an Arctic temperature increase which is partly damped by the enhanced heat loss through the sea surface, as found in other climate models.”

In terms of individual gateways, the BSO provides 41% of the total increase in OHT into the Arctic Ocean between 1961-1980 and 2081-2100. The OHT also increases through the Fram and Bering straits, while the Nares Strait OHT is fairly constant until about 2040 when it starts to decrease, and volume transport declines slightly across the Bering Strait.

While thermodynamic (i.e. temperature-driven) changes largely drive the net OHT increase into the Arctic, nonlinear components (i.e. anomalies due to concurrent changes in temperature and velocity) also play a major role. Of the net OHT increase from 1920-80 to 2081-2100, thermodynamic changes contribute 0.03 PW, with nonlinear changes contributing 0.01 PW; dynamic circulation changes act to decrease the net OHT after 2040, with an anomaly slightly smaller than -0.01 PW over the same period due to negative dynamic components from the Nares and Barrow Straits.

The research also looked into the impacts of shortwave (solar) and longwave radiation on the ocean and on sea ice, and looks at the heat budget from the perspective of the ice.

“Essentially, the heat transported into the Arctic Ocean via OHT is primarily used to melt the sea ice until the sea ice coverage declines substantially in the mid-21st century and the exposed ocean surface increases, after which heat begins to flux out to the atmosphere,” the researchers noted.

In terms of heat flux components, while absorbed shortwave radiation strengthens due to decreasing surface albedo with more open ocean and reduced cloud cover, starting in 2040 this increased heat flux is compensated by strengthened outgoing longwave radiation and stronger sensible and latent heat loss reflecting ocean warming and more extended open waters, according to the research. Though incoming longwave radiation also increases over the course of the simulations, that increase is compensated by the strengthened outgoing longwave radiation, which is consistent with the balance in the mean seasonal cycle and which explains the increased ocean cooling due to longwave radiation out to 2100.

“It is very important to understand why the Arctic Ocean is warming and why there are dramatic changes that are being predicted,” Oldenburg said. “This research, which reinforces what has already been found about extreme warming in the Arctic and the loss of sea ice, highlights the importance of ocean heat transport in driving Arctic warming and sea ice decline.”

TITLE: Press Release -Strengthening the Capacity of Africa’s Science Granting Councils in Research Management

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Nairobi, Kenya and Accra, Ghana (17 August 2020) – Africa faces some of the world’s greatest development challenges and its research capacity is not yet sufficient to meet them. Improving research management within institutions is crucial, if research and innovation is to underpin social and economic development in Africa.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is collaborating with the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) to implement the second phase of the Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI) Research Management Project which will strengthen the capacities of Africa’s Science Granting Councils to play their essential roles effectively and efficiently in research, knowledge generation and innovation through training, technical support, and peer-to-peer learning.

Building on the success of the first phase of the SGCI, the Research Management Project is being implemented in 15 sub Saharan African countries, specifically in Ghana, Burkina Faso, Cote d’Ivoire, Senegal, Botswana, Malawi, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Ethiopia, Namibia, and Rwanda. The project will support the development of research and evidence-based policies that will contribute to economic and social development on the continent.

“The overall goal of the project is to fortify the capability of Science Granting Councils in explicit areas of research management, namely research excellence, research ethics, emerging scientific practices (especially open data, open access and scientific citizenship) and development of online grant management systems” said Prof Jonathan Mba, Director of Research and Academic Planning at the AAU.

“Our participation in this project is to complement our efforts to address systemic gaps in the broad research ecosystem so as to create and sustain research environments that enable research to flourish.” said Allen Mukhwana, Research Systems Manager at the AAS.

Africa’s Science Granting Councils are key players and strategic partners in improving the continent’s scientific research outputs and achieving continental policy initiatives such as the African Union’s Science, Technology, and Innovation Strategy for Africa 2024 (STISA-2024), and the Continental Education Strategy for Africa 2016-2025 (CESA 16-25). It is therefore critical that their capacity in research management is regularly built in areas where gaps have been identified. With strengthened capacities in research management, Science Granting Councils in Africa will better play their crucial roles as integrators and brokers of knowledge within their national systems of innovation.

The SGCI is a multi-funder initiative that is funded by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida), United Kingdom’s Department for International Development (DFID), Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC), South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF) and the German Research Foundation (DFG).

The Association of African Universities and the African Academy of Sciences are strongly committed to working closely with the Science Granting Councils to achieve ‘Research Excellence’ as reflected in their strategic plans. The AAU’s 2020 -2025 Strategic Plan, for instance, prioritizes closer engagement with national policy systems in African Countries, whilst the AAS Strategy emphasizes strengthening of African institutions to become excellent and adaptable to proven needs.

AAU aims to improve the quality of African higher education, and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting higher education.
